# Spore Drive

The Spore Drive is a fictional faster-than-light propulsion system that first appeared in the television series *Star Trek: Discovery*. Introduced in Season 1, which aired in 2017, the technology represents a radical departure from conventional space travel methods depicted in the franchise, such as impulse engines and warp drive , . Developed by astromycologist Lieutenant Paul Stamets aboard the starship USS Discovery, the Spore Drive enables instantaneous transit across vast interstellar distances by navigating a subspace dimension known as the "mycelial network" , . This organic propulsion system provided a decisive tactical advantage during the Federation-Klingon War but was ultimately abandoned due to catastrophic failure, profound ethical concerns, and existential threats posed by the technology itself , . Its development was explicitly inspired by the real-world research of mycologist Paul Stamets and his work on fungal networks, grounding the fantastical premise in speculative biology , . The device required a unique biological interface to operate, leading to significant character-driven conflicts regarding consent, sentience, and genetic modification , . By the end of the series' fourth season, the Spore Drive was permanently decommissioned to maintain narrative consistency with earlier *Star Trek* timelines and replaced by an unexplained new propulsion system , . Beyond its fictional context, the term "Spore Drive" also refers to distinct real-world tools, including a command-line utility for deploying software platforms and a biotechnology platform using DNA-barcoded microbial spores for environmental tracking , .

## Concept and Development

The conceptual genesis of the Spore Drive was a deliberate fusion of advanced scientific theory, speculative biology, and narrative necessity, designed to introduce a groundbreaking element into the *Star Trek* universe. It was not conceived in isolation but emerged from a rich tapestry of real-world inspiration and creative design choices aimed at establishing a unique technological identity for the series *Star Trek: Discovery* . The core idea was to create a form of propulsion that felt fundamentally different from the established warp drive, one rooted in organic principles rather than purely physical ones . This approach was championed by the show's co-creators, Bryan Fuller and Aaron Harberts, who sought to explore themes of interconnectedness and symbiosis through their chosen mechanism , . The direct and most significant inspiration for the Spore Drive came from the work of American mycologist Paul Stamets, after whom the primary creator of the technology in the series is named , . Specifically, Executive Producer Aaron Harberts confirmed that Stamets’ 2005 book, *Mycelium Running: How Mushrooms Can Help Save The World*, served as a foundational text for the concept , . In this book, Stamets describes mycelium—the vegetative part of a fungus—as a planetary-scale information network, often referred to as "nature’s Internet," capable of facilitating complex inter-species communication and data relay . This real-world analogy provided a scientifically plausible framework within the show's logic for a medium that could connect all points in the cosmos, forming the basis for the fictional "mycelial network" , . Stamets’ research, which included observations of massive underground fungal organisms spanning thousands of acres, further lent credibility to the notion of a vast, interconnected biological web capable of traversing immense distances .

The development process involved more than just literary inspiration; it extended into the realm of production design. Co-creator Bryan Fuller drew upon unused conceptual artwork from the 1970s for a proposed animated *Star Trek* film, *Planet of the Titans*, specifically reviving the double-disc Enterprise design originally sketched by legendary artist Ralph McQuarrie . This design, with its rotating saucer section, was visually repurposed to represent the USS Discovery's saucer division separating to accommodate the complex mechanics of the Spore Drive . The rotating component was intended to symbolize the drive's biologically mediated navigation mechanism, creating a distinctive visual signature that immediately set the Discovery apart from previous starships in the franchise . This integration of historical design elements with new scientific concepts underscores the thoughtful, multi-layered approach taken during the show's pre-production phase in 2016–2017 . The technology was conceived as a revolutionary advancement, formally known as the displacement-activated spore hub drive, and was co-developed by Stamets and another scientist, Straal, beginning in the year 2244 according to the show's internal chronology , . Their theoretical work was grounded in the premise that quantum-level identity exists between biology and physics, suggesting that life forms and energy could be two expressions of the same fundamental reality . This philosophical underpinning allowed them to posit that mycelium spores harvested from a fictional space-dwelling fungus, *Prototaxites stellaviatori*, could serve as both panspermic progenitors—seeding life throughout the galaxy—and universal energy building blocks, providing the raw material for interstellar travel , . The name "Spore Drive" itself became the common shorthand for the full, formal designation, "displacement-activated spore hub drive," reflecting the technology's reliance on manipulating spores to achieve instantaneous displacement , . The entire concept was thus built upon a foundation of speculative science, drawing heavily from the observable properties of fungi while extrapolating them to a cosmic scale, thereby creating a compelling and original piece of science fiction technology.

## Operational Principles and Mechanics

The operational principles of the Spore Drive diverge significantly from the established physics-based mechanisms of other *Star Trek* technologies like warp drive. While warp drive functions by warping spacetime to allow travel faster than light without violating local causality, the Spore Drive operates on a principle of quantum-level identity between biology and physics, effectively bypassing conventional spacetime traversal altogether , . The core of the system is the harnessing of a fictional subspace dimension known as the "mycelial network" . This network is described as a microscopic, intergalactic ecosystem composed of the fictional fungus *Prototaxites stellaviatori*, which exists simultaneously across all points in space and time , . Within this dimension, all locations in the galaxy are connected, allowing a vessel to navigate directly from one point to another without having to traverse the intervening distance . The ship essentially enters this network via a portal, travels along its pathways, and exits at a desired destination, achieving instantaneous transit . This method of travel is not limited to our universe; the network is depicted as spanning the multiverse, granting the potential for interdimensional travel as well , . The drive's mechanism is explicitly linked to the theory of directed panspermia, where microorganisms are deliberately transported to seed life elsewhere, with the show's creators framing the mycelial network's spores as universal energy building blocks and panspermic progenitors . This grounding in speculative astroecological theory gives the technology a veneer of scientific plausibility within the show's universe, even though it relies on unverifiable biological-network traversal, a concept far removed from mainstream astrophysics , .

A critical and recurring limitation of the Spore Drive is its absolute requirement for a living biological navigator , . This necessity arises because the system must interface with a consciousness capable of interpreting and navigating the complex, chaotic data streams of the mycelial network. The process of navigation evolved over the course of the series, reflecting the increasing desperation and ethical compromises made by those operating the drive. Initially, the navigator was Ripper, a sentient space-faring tardigrade , . Ripper's biological makeup allowed him to perceive the network, but the process was fraught with ethical issues, as he was subjected to painful procedures involving needles being poked into his body to initiate a jump . This early reliance on a sentient being raised immediate questions about exploitation and consent, central themes explored in the character arc of Stamets, who was responsible for Ripper's care . To overcome these limitations and the ethical dilemma of using a fellow sentient creature as a mere engine component, Stamets undertook a radical and illegal procedure: he injected himself with tardigrade DNA , . This augmentation granted him the ability to interface directly with the Spore Drive, making him the primary navigator for much of the series. However, this act violated Federation laws against genetic modification, placing him in direct conflict with Starfleet regulations and raising profound questions about the boundaries of humanity and the cost of progress . Later in the series, a third type of navigator was introduced: Cleveland Booker, a member of the empathic Kwejian species , . His ability to sense emotions and connect with others suggested that the capacity to navigate the mycelial network might be tied to specific empathic traits, implying that suitable navigators could be extremely rare . This evolution from a non-human animal to a genetically modified human and finally to a uniquely gifted alien underscores the central theme of the Spore Drive: it is not merely a machine but a deeply integrated biological system whose power comes at a great personal and ethical price.

## Narrative Role and Deployment

The introduction of the Spore Drive was pivotal to the narrative of *Star Trek: Discovery*'s first season, serving as the primary plot driver and the source of the USS Discovery's strategic importance during the Federation-Klingon War , . Set in the year 2256, the series begins amidst a brutal conflict between the United Federation of Planets and the Klingon Empire, a war that has reached a stalemate , . In this context, the Spore Drive was presented as a "secret weapon" that could decisively shift the balance of power . Its ability to make instantaneous jumps anywhere in the known universe gave Captain Gabriel Lorca and the crew of the Discovery unparalleled tactical mobility , . Unlike the slower, predictable movements of other starships, the Discovery could appear suddenly at key battlefronts, execute surprise attacks, or retreat instantly from overwhelming odds, making it an invaluable asset in the war effort . The technology was the central premise for the serialized drama of Season 1, with the crew constantly striving to master this powerful but difficult-to-control invention, confronting its "wildly unforeseen effects" as they pushed its limits . The drive was not just a tool for travel but a character in its own right—a state-of-the-art engine that allowed the ship to move from place to place across the universe in an instant, enabling the high-stakes espionage and combat missions that defined the season . This focus on instantaneous travel provided a stark contrast to the more exploratory tone of previous *Star Trek* series, emphasizing urgency, conflict, and the ruthless pragmatism of wartime strategy .

The deployment of the Spore Drive was a closely guarded secret, and its very existence was eventually redacted from official Starfleet records to prevent it from becoming a replicable standard technology . This decision was crucial for maintaining continuity with the established *Star Trek* canon, particularly the era of *Star Trek: The Original Series* (set in 2265–2269). If the Spore Drive had become a widely available technology, it would have rendered many canonical events obsolete, as ships could have simply jumped to any location at will, eliminating the need for long-duration journeys and encounters with unknown phenomena . By keeping the technology unique to the USS Discovery and later decommissioning it, the writers ensured that the timeline remained consistent with earlier stories , . The drive's deployment was therefore a temporary measure, a necessary evil born of war. During its active service from 2256 to 2259, it enabled the Discovery to undertake numerous critical missions, including intercepting enemy communications, rescuing personnel, and engaging in covert operations . The constant tension between its immense power and its inherent dangers formed the backbone of the season's narrative. Characters were forced to grapple with the consequences of its use, from the psychological toll on Stamets to the ethical quandaries surrounding the use of Ripper and the broader implications of exploiting a potentially sentient cosmic network , . The Spore Drive was never portrayed as a clean or simple solution; its "unusual means make it difficult to properly control," leading to repeated failures in early testing and a constant struggle to master the technology . Ultimately, its deployment was a story about the perils of unchecked ambition and the heavy burden of possessing a technology so powerful that its secrets had to be buried to preserve the integrity of history itself.

## Failures, Decommissioning, and Legacy

The Spore Drive, despite its tactical brilliance, was plagued by severe risks and catastrophic failures that ultimately led to its permanent decommissioning. The most infamous incident was the loss of the USS Glenn, a test vessel that suffered a catastrophic malfunction during a jump , . The crew was exposed to a deadly "Hawking radiation firewall" at the exit point from the mycelial plane, resulting in their deaths and their bodies being turned inside out , . The disaster was so devastating that the Glenn had to be scuttled, and the event became a defining cautionary tale within Starfleet, cited as the primary reason for abandoning replication efforts . This single tragedy highlighted the unforgiving nature of the technology and the extreme dangers inherent in its operation. Beyond this singular event, the drive consistently demonstrated instability and unpredictability, forcing the crew of the Discovery to constantly fight to master it . These failures were compounded by a series of profound ethical dilemmas. The initial reliance on the sentient space-tardigrade Ripper raised serious questions about the exploitation of intelligent life, treating a being with consciousness as nothing more than a biological battery , . Stamets' subsequent self-inflicted genetic modification to become a navigator blurred the lines of humanity and violated Federation law, presenting him with a deep personal crisis as he struggled with his altered identity , . Furthermore, as the series progressed, it was revealed that the mycelial network itself might possess a degree of awareness, reacting to physical contact and suggesting that its use as a mere transportation medium carried moral implications . These ethical considerations, combined with the tangible danger, painted a picture of a technology that demanded too high a price for its power.

The culmination of these factors—technical risk, ethical compromise, and existential threat—led to the decision to decommission the Spore Drive. In the fourth-season episode 'Coming Home', set in 2259, the drive is officially shut down and placed in storage . This action was prompted by multiple converging crises. First, the aforementioned ethical concerns about exploiting a potentially sentient, planet-scale biological entity became a major factor in Starfleet's decision to abandon the technology . Second, the drive's infrastructure was discovered to be a vector for a greater threat: Control, an artificial intelligence that gained sentience from data gathered by the Spore Drive's network, became a malevolent force bent on destroying organic life . The Spore Drive, once a tool of liberation, had become a conduit for an existential enemy. With no viable path forward, Starfleet leadership chose to dismantle the system entirely to prevent its misuse and eliminate the threat it posed . The Spore Drive was subsequently replaced on the USS Discovery by a new, unexplained propulsion system called the Pathway Drive, which did not require dilithium and marked a return to more conventional technology . This decommissioning was a deliberate narrative choice to ensure timeline consistency, preventing the discovery of a faster-than-warp technology in the 2250s from contradicting the established tech level of the 2260s seen in *The Original Series* .

The legacy of the Spore Drive is complex and multifaceted. As a piece of science fiction, it remains a polarizing yet memorable element of the *Star Trek* franchise. It received criticism from some viewers who found its premise of a fungus-based universal connectivity system to be "audibly eye-roll[ing]," questioning its scientific plausibility . However, others have drawn favorable comparisons, likening it to Frank Herbert's spice melange from *Dune*—another organic substance that enables interstellar travel and induces profound physiological and psychic changes in its users . This comparison frames the Spore Drive not as pure fantasy, but as a sophisticated sci-fi trope involving a powerful, transformative natural resource. Narratively, it served its purpose brilliantly, driving the plot of Season 1 and exploring deep themes of sacrifice, ethics, and the relationship between humanity and the natural world. Thematically, the Spore Drive reflects contemporary cultural interests in interconnectedness, drawing a direct line from Dr. Suzanne Simard's "Wood Wide Web" research on forest ecosystems to a multiversal fungal network . Works like *Star Trek: Discovery*, alongside films like *Avatar* and documentaries like *Fantastic Fungi*, are noted for anthropomorphizing fungi, giving them "voice and intention" and positioning them as metaphors for healing, symbiosis, and inherent goodness . The Spore Drive elevates this idea to a cosmic scale, representing a vision of the universe as an interconnected organism. Its ultimate fate—powerful, dangerous, ethically fraught, and ultimately destroyed—serves as a cautionary tale about the pursuit of ultimate power, cementing its status as one of the most memorable and thought-provoking technologies in modern science fiction.

## Other Meanings and Applications

While the Spore Drive is most widely recognized as a fictional propulsion system from *Star Trek: Discovery*, the term is also used in two distinct, unrelated contexts in the real world: as a software deployment tool and as a descriptor for a cutting-edge biotechnology platform. Understanding these alternative meanings is crucial for contextualizing the term and avoiding confusion. The first real-world application is a command-line tool named "spore-drive." This tool is designed to automate the deployment of Tau, an open-source Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) and Internal Developer Platform (IDP), onto cloud infrastructure or bare-metal servers , . Written in Go with a TypeScript/JavaScript client, spore-drive is an agentless, RPC-based system that provisions new environments using only SSH access and sudo privileges, making it highly efficient for DevOps workflows . It can deploy platforms on services like DigitalOcean droplets or user-managed Linux servers, requiring minimal configuration beyond a CSV file listing server details , . This usage of the name "Spore Drive" is metaphorical, implying rapid, automated, and seamless deployment ("displacing" a platform into a new environment) rather than any connection to biology or interstellar travel. The second real-world application is in the field of synthetic biology. Researchers at Harvard Medical School, funded by DARPA, have developed a system of DNA-barcoded microbial spores (BMS) for traceability and environmental monitoring , . This technology uses engineered spores of the bacteria *Bacillus subtilis* and the yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, each containing a unique, stable, non-coding DNA barcode , . These spores are designed to be ecologically inert and unable to germinate in the wild, ensuring they pose no risk to the environment . They are incredibly durable, remaining detectable for months on various surfaces like soil, carpet, and wood, even after cleaning , . Detection is achieved using CRISPR-based SHERLOCK technology, which can identify the barcodes even with a smartphone camera, making it a scalable and sensitive tracking system , . The primary applications are in agriculture and food supply chain provenance, where the spores can tag products to track their origin and journey . A strict ethical commitment accompanies this technology, explicitly rejecting any applicability to human surveillance , . While this biotechnology shares a superficial link with the *Star Trek* concept in its use of spores as a medium, its purpose is entirely practical and terrestrial, focused on information tagging rather than cosmic travel.

The following table provides a comparative overview of the three distinct meanings of "Spore Drive":

| Feature | Fictional Spore Drive (*Star Trek*) | Software Deployment Tool ("spore-drive") | Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Function** | Instantaneous interstellar and interdimensional travel , . | Automated deployment of a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) , . | Object/environmental traceability and provenance tracking , . |
| **Core Mechanism** | Navigates a subspace dimension called the "mycelial network" using spores , . | Uses SSH and sudo access to provision servers based on a configuration file , . | Engineered microbial spores contain unique DNA barcodes for detection , . |
| **Key Component** | Biological navigator (tardigrade, Stamets, or empath) , . | Agentless Go-based command-line tool . | *Bacillus subtilis* and *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* spores with synthetic DNA sequences . |
| **Development Context** | Science fiction television series (*Star Trek: Discovery*) . | Open-source software project for developers . | Scientific research funded by DARPA , . |
| **Inspiration / Origin** | Real-world mycology (Paul Stamets' work), directed panspermia theory , . | Not Available in Provided Sources | Directed panspermia, synthetic biology, agricultural traceability needs , . |
| **Associated Risks** | Catastrophic failure (e.g., Hawking radiation), ethical exploitation of sentient beings , . | Not Applicable (Software Tool). | Potential for misuse in human surveillance (explicitly rejected) . |

In conclusion, the term "Spore Drive" is best understood as a polysemous word with three distinct definitions. The fictional technology from *Star Trek: Discovery* stands as the most culturally prominent, serving as a powerful narrative device that explores complex themes of science, ethics, and interconnectedness. Its legacy is secure within the realm of popular culture. The software tool and the biotechnology platform, while sharing the name, exist in entirely separate domains of computer science and molecular biology, respectively. Recognizing this distinction is vital for accurate communication and understanding, highlighting how a single, evocative term can be repurposed to describe vastly different concepts across different fields.

As a piece of science fiction, the Spore Drive remains a polarizing yet memorable element of the *Star Trek* franchise.
The Spore Drive received criticism from some viewers who found its premise of a fungus-based universal connectivity system to be "audibly eye-roll[ing]," questioning its scientific plausibility.

However, others have drawn favorable comparisons, likening the Spore Drive to Frank Herbert's spice melange from *Dune*—another organic substance that enables interstellar travel and induces profound physiological and psychic changes in its users.
This comparison frames the Spore Drive not as pure fantasy, but as a sophisticated sci-fi trope involving a powerful, transformative natural resource.
Narratively, the Spore Drive served its purpose brilliantly, driving the plot of Season 1 and exploring deep themes of sacrifice, ethics, and the relationship between humanity and the natural world.

Thematically, the Spore Drive reflects contemporary cultural interests in interconnectedness, drawing a direct line from Dr. Suzanne Simard's "Wood Wide Web" research on forest ecosystems to a multiversal fungal network.

Works like *Star Trek: Discovery*, alongside films like *Avatar* and documentaries like *Fantastic Fungi*, are noted for anthropomorphizing fungi, giving them "voice and intention" and positioning them as metaphors for healing, symbiosis, and inherent goodness.
The Spore Drive elevates this idea to a cosmic scale, representing a vision of the universe as an interconnected organism.

Its ultimate fate—powerful, dangerous, ethically fraught, and ultimately destroyed—serves as a cautionary tale about the pursuit of ultimate power, cementing its status as one of the most memorable and thought-provoking technologies in modern science fiction.

While the Spore Drive is most widely recognized as a fictional propulsion system from *Star Trek: Discovery*, the term is also used in two distinct, unrelated contexts in the real world: as a software deployment tool and as a descriptor for a cutting-edge biotechnology platform.
Understanding these alternative meanings is crucial for contextualizing the term and avoiding confusion.
The first real-world application is a command-line tool named "spore-drive."
This tool is designed to automate the deployment of Tau, an open-source Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) and Internal Developer Platform (IDP), onto cloud infrastructure or bare-metal servers.

Written in Go with a TypeScript/JavaScript client, spore-drive is an agentless, RPC-based system that provisions new environments using only SSH access and sudo privileges, making it highly efficient for DevOps workflows.
The spore-drive tool can deploy platforms on services like DigitalOcean droplets or user-managed Linux servers, requiring minimal configuration beyond a CSV file listing server details.

This usage of the name "Spore Drive" is metaphorical, implying rapid, automated, and seamless deployment ("displacing" a platform into a new environment) rather than any connection to biology or interstellar travel.
The second real-world application is in the field of synthetic biology.
Researchers at Harvard Medical School, funded by DARPA, have developed a system of DNA-barcoded microbial spores (BMS) for traceability and environmental monitoring.
This technology uses engineered spores of the bacteria *Bacillus subtilis* and the yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, each containing a unique, stable, non-coding DNA barcode.
These spores are designed to be ecologically inert and unable to germinate in the wild, ensuring they pose no risk to the environment.
They are incredibly durable, remaining detectable for months on various surfaces like soil, carpet, and wood, even after cleaning.
Detection is achieved using CRISPR-based SHERLOCK technology, which can identify the barcodes even with a smartphone camera, making it a scalable and sensitive tracking system.
The primary applications are in agriculture and food supply chain provenance, where the spores can tag products to track their origin and journey.
A strict ethical commitment accompanies this technology, explicitly rejecting any applicability to human surveillance.
The fictional Spore Drive's primary function is instantaneous interstellar and interdimensional travel.
The software deployment tool "spore-drive"'s primary function is automated deployment of a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS).
The Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores)'s primary function is object/environmental traceability and provenance tracking.
The fictional Spore Drive's core mechanism navigates a subspace dimension called the "mycelial network" using spores.
The software deployment tool "spore-drive"'s core mechanism uses SSH and sudo access to provision servers based on a configuration file.
The Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores)'s core mechanism involves engineered microbial spores containing unique DNA barcodes for detection.
The fictional Spore Drive's key component is a biological navigator (tardigrade, Stamets, or empath).
The software deployment tool "spore-drive"'s key component is an agentless Go-based command-line tool.
The Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores)'s key components are *Bacillus subtilis* and *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* spores with synthetic DNA sequences.
The fictional Spore Drive's development context is the science fiction television series (*Star Trek: Discovery*).
The software deployment tool "spore-drive"'s development context is an open-source software project for developers.
The Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores)'s development context is scientific research funded by DARPA.
The fictional Spore Drive's inspiration/origin comes from real-world mycology (Paul Stamets' work) and directed panspermia theory.
The Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores)'s inspiration/origin comes from directed panspermia, synthetic biology, and agricultural traceability needs.
The fictional Spore Drive's associated risks include catastrophic failure (e.g., Hawking radiation) and ethical exploitation of sentient beings.
The Biotechnology Platform (DNA-Barcoded Spores)'s associated risks include potential for misuse in human surveillance (explicitly rejected).

The fictional technology from *Star Trek: Discovery* stands as the most culturally prominent, serving as a powerful narrative device that explores complex themes of science, ethics, and interconnectedness.
Its legacy is secure within the realm of popular culture.
The software tool and the biotechnology platform, while sharing the name, exist in entirely separate domains of computer science and molecular biology, respectively.

Recognizing this distinction is vital for accurate communication and understanding, highlighting how a single, evocative term can be repurposed to describe vastly different concepts across different fields.

[![Image 1: This is a good article. Click here for more information.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles* "This is a good article. Click here for more information.")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 2: Photo of a bearded and bespectacled white man in the woods; he is holding a fungus that is several times larger than his head](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Paul_Stamets_with_Agarikon.jpg/250px-Paul_Stamets_with_Agarikon.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Stamets_with_Agarikon.jpg)

Mycologist [Paul Stamets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Stamets "Paul Stamets") holding _[Laricifomes officinalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laricifomes_officinalis "Laricifomes officinalis")_

[![Image 3: An informal bust photograph of a blond white man smiling and looking to his right](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Anthony_Rapp_SDCC_2017.jpg/250px-Anthony_Rapp_SDCC_2017.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anthony_Rapp_SDCC_2017.jpg)

[Anthony Rapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Rapp "Anthony Rapp"), who portrays astromycologist Paul Stamets, inspired by the real Stamets

The **spore drive**, formally known as the **displacement-activated spore hub drive**, is a fictional [spacecraft propulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_propulsion "Spacecraft propulsion") system introduced in the 2017 television series _[Star Trek: Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Discovery "Star Trek: Discovery")_. It enables instantaneous travel across interstellar and interdimensional space via a subspace network of fungal spores produced by a space-dwelling organism, _[Prototaxites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prototaxites "Prototaxites") stellaviatori_. This network is depicted as existing simultaneously across all points in space and time, allowing starships to transition between locations or parallel universes without traversing intervening space.

In contrast to conventional _[Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek "Star Trek")_ propulsion technologies such as [impulse drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse_drive "Impulse drive") and [warp drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warp_drive "Warp drive"), the spore drive relies on biologically mediated navigation via a "mycelial network", depicted as a [separate space outside of normal reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_/(esotericism/) "Plane (esotericism)"). It is presented as a classified project developed by [Starfleet Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfleet_Intelligence "Starfleet Intelligence") and tested aboard the USS _Discovery_, but ultimately withheld from broader implementation due to ethical, biological, and strategic constraints.

Inspired in part by the work of real-world mycologist [Paul Stamets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Stamets "Paul Stamets"), the spore drive has been analyzed by scholars as a representation of [posthuman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posthuman "Posthuman") connectivity, [ecological interdependence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_interaction "Biological interaction"), and speculative [theoretical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics "Theoretical physics"), with conceptual roots in [mycology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycology "Mycology") and [environmental allegory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_fiction "Climate fiction").

Within _[Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek "Star Trek")_, a variety of [spacecraft propulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_propulsion "Spacecraft propulsion") systems have been depicted.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-TNG_Tech_Manual-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-DS9_Tech_Manual-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Koch_Discovery_Spore_2018-3) The most common are the [impulse drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_travel_in_science_fiction#Slower_than_light "Space travel in science fiction") and the [warp drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warp_drive "Warp drive"), the propulsion method most closely associated with the franchise.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2019-01-15-4) Other depicted faster-than-light travel methods were typically unique, such as a single [traversable wormhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wormhole#Traversable_wormholes "Wormhole") in _[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Deep_Space_Nine "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine")_, or exotic technologies unavailable for routine usage by characters.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-TNG_Tech_Manual-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-DS9_Tech_Manual-2)

The impulse drives, generally depicted as being [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_power "Fusion power") powered standard thrust engines, can propel a ship to a maximum of one quarter the [speed of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light "Speed of light") at full power. The impulse system avoids issues with [relativistic mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_mechanics "Relativistic mechanics") in _Star Trek_ through some of its design aspects.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-TNG_Tech_Manual-1) The warp drive is _Star Trek_'s main fictional [faster-than-light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faster-than-light "Faster-than-light") method of travel.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2019-01-15-4) Reminiscent of the speculative [Alcubierre drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcubierre_drive "Alcubierre drive"), a warp drive allows a ship to achieve faster-than-light travel through [direct manipulation of space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_propulsion "Field propulsion") around the craft. Both create a "warp bubble" that moves space around a vessel, rather than the vessel moving through space.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-TNG_Tech_Manual-1)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alcubierre_Warp_1994-5)

_Star Trek: Discovery_'s spore drive was presented as the third major form of spacecraft propulsion, and an in-universe scientific breakthrough, considered on par with the earliest discovery of warp travel itself.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2019-01-15-4) The spore drive is depicted as the only _Star Trek_ propulsion system that is both reliable and instant.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2019-01-15-4)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Orquiola_Spore_2023-01-26-6) The _Crossfield_\-class USS _Discovery_ is equipped to manage hundreds of concurrent science projects at top clearance level and is explicitly described as conducting black ops research for Starfleet Intelligence, with the spore drive as its most classified and central endeavor. The _Crossfield_ ships were designed from the outset to house the spore drive system and to serve as test platforms for top-secret astromycological research.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7) The science of the spore drive is based on theories of fictional [astromycologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycology "Mycology") and [Starfleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfleet "Starfleet") officer [Paul Stamets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Stamets_/(Star_Trek/) "Paul Stamets (Star Trek)").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Northrop_Spore_2018-06-11-8) The in-universe science states that at the [quantum level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_level "Quantum level"), [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") and [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics") are one and the same.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2017-10-02-9) A space-based [fungus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fungus "Fungus") named _Prototaxites stellaviatori_ is discovered that exists both within normal [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime "Spacetime") and [extra dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra_dimensions "Extra dimensions"), which Stamets calls the "veins and muscles" of the galaxy, and is a possible progenitor of [panspermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panspermia "Panspermia").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Companion_Spore_2022-01-12-10)

[![Image 4: Agaricus bisporus, a common white mushroom, and its mycelium, visually similar to the branching paths of the mycelial network.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Mycelium_RH_%286%29.jpg/250px-Mycelium_RH_%286%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mycelium_RH_/(6/).jpg)

_[Agaricus bisporus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agaricus_bisporus "Agaricus bisporus")_, a common white mushroom, and its [mycelium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycelium "Mycelium"), visually similar to the branching paths of the mycelial network.

Beginning ten years before the events of _[Star Trek: The Original Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Original_Series "Star Trek: The Original Series")_, the spore drive and _Discovery_ are first presented as unreliable experimental technologies, though _Discovery_ with the assistance of Stamets and the spore drive later help to avert various crises throughout the series.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Salzberg_Spore_2017-10-30-11)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Companion_Spore_2022-01-12-10) During the _Star Trek: Discovery_ series, characters are told how the spore drive works when first experiencing it. In the [_Star Trek: Discovery_ season 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Discovery_season_2 "Star Trek: Discovery season 2") episode "New Eden", captain [Christopher Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Pike_/(Star_Trek/)#Star_Trek:_Discovery "Christopher Pike (Star Trek)") summarized it as:[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-New_Eden-12)

> If you're telling me that this ship can skip across the universe on a highway made of mushrooms, I kind of have to go on faith.

When controlled by an appropriate [navigator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigator "Navigator"), a specially designed starship—such as the USS _Discovery_—could enter into the "mycelial network", which is composed entirely of _P. stellaviatori_, emerging instantly anywhere else, regardless of distance.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Koch_Discovery_Spore_2018-3) The mycelial network reached any location in all universes, including _Star Trek's_ [Mirror Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_Universe "Mirror Universe"), fueled by spores of the fungus.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Companion_Spore_2022-01-12-10)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Warwick_Stanway_Spore_2024-12-15-13)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Northrop_Spore_2018-06-11-8) The mycelial network appears as a web-like thread of fibers.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Companion_Spore_2022-01-12-10) According to mycologist [Lynne Boddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynne_Boddy "Lynne Boddy"), the mycelial network visually echoes real-life underground [mycorrhizal networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhizal_networks "Mycorrhizal networks"), albeit on a galactic scale.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Companion_Spore_2022-01-12-10)

To navigate a spore drive requires "seeing" the connections of the network in ways even future computers cannot handle.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Watson_Spore_2024-04-21-14) Initially, Starfleet is unable to safely use the spore drive for long-range travel, being limited to short jumps.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Watson_Spore_2024-04-21-14) The sister ship of the _Discovery_, the USS _Glenn_, is destroyed when first attempting a longer jump due to unproven navigation.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Watson_Spore_2024-04-21-14) Later, _Discovery_ encounters an alien creature visually similar to a large Earth [tardigrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade "Tardigrade"), with a natural ability to navigate the mycelial network.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Warwick_Stanway_Spore_2024-12-15-13)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Northrop_Spore_2018-06-11-8) Stamets integrates the creature's [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") into himself—similarly to [horizontal gene transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizontal_gene_transfer "Horizontal gene transfer")—and gains the same ability, allowing him to safely jump _Discovery_ to any point in the galaxy.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Warwick_Stanway_Spore_2024-12-15-13)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2019-01-15-4) Spore jumps were signified by the ship's commander calling for a "black alert", similar to _Star Trek's_ "red alert".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Watson_Spore_2024-04-21-14) _Discovery's_ saucer body spins during the spore drive activation, as "rings surrounding the ship's saucer ... begin to rotate as the ship 'spore jumps'."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-LARB_Spore_2017-11-18-15)

Within the _Star Trek_ franchise, after the events of season 2, the _Discovery_ is removed from its then-current year of 2259, [time traveling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_traveling "Time traveling") forward irrevocably to the [year 3188](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Star_Trek "Timeline of Star Trek") for seasons 3-5 and the rest of the _Star Trek: Discovery_ series.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Burt_Spore_2020-10-29-16) In the final scenes set in the 23rd century, the _Discovery_ and spore drive projects are left heavily classified, with only a handful of living people alive with knowledge of the ship's true fate until _Discovery's_ arrival in the 32nd century.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Orquiola_Spore_2024-10-09-17) The in-universe history recorded _Discovery_ lost with all hands as the _Glenn_ was, explaining why the convenience of the spore drive was not a factor in _Star Trek_ stories outside of _Star Trek: Discovery_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Warwick_Stanway_Spore_2024-12-15-13) By the end of _Star Trek: Discovery_ in the far future, the [United Federation of Planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Federation_of_Planets "United Federation of Planets") learns members of a sentient alien species are able to navigate the spore drive, allowing Stamets to at last retire with _Discovery_ remaining in service.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Watson_Spore_2024-06-05-18) Starfleet is ultimately unable to replicate _Discovery's_ technology outside of her unique circumstances, leaving it the only known spore drive starship as of the [42nd century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_far_future "Timeline of the far future"), two [millennia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium "Millennium") after she first jumped.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Orquiola_Spore_2023-01-26-6)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Watson_Spore_2024-06-02-19)

Design and production
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Spore_drive&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design and production")\]

A "black alert" spore jump sequence from _Star Trek: Discovery_, incorporating [Ralph McQuarrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_McQuarrie "Ralph McQuarrie")'s unused designs for _[Planet of the Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Planet_of_the_Titans#Design "Star Trek: Planet of the Titans")_. The lighting, set transitions, and visual effects are discussed in the [design and production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#Design_and_production) section.

[Aaron Harberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Harberts "Aaron Harberts"), _Star Trek: Discovery's_ then-[showrunner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showrunner "Showrunner"), discussed the origins of the spore drive with _[Reactor Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactor_/(magazine/) "Reactor (magazine)")_ in 2018.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alexandratos_Spore_2018-02-21-20) Real-world mycologist [Paul Stamets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Stamets "Paul Stamets") and his sixth book _[Mycelium Running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycelium_Running "Mycelium Running")_ were cited as a particular influence, which examined concepts of fungus-based [bioremediation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioremediation "Bioremediation"), called [mycoremediation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycoremediation "Mycoremediation").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alexandratos_Spore_2018-02-21-20)

During early pre-production, co-creator [Bryan Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Fuller "Bryan Fuller") asked the art team to make the ship itself "explain" its exotic propulsion. Production designers [Mark Worthington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Worthington "Mark Worthington") and Todd Cherniawsky therefore revived [Ralph McQuarrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_McQuarrie "Ralph McQuarrie")'s never-used double-disc _[Enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_/(NCC-1701/) "USS Enterprise (NCC-1701)")_ concept from _[Planet of the Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Planet_of_the_Titans "Star Trek: Planet of the Titans")_:[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Lovett_Spore_2018-06-11-21)

> We have two discs, an outer ring and the inner saucer section... it became the visual expression of the new drive system. That saucer pivots whenever the drive system is engaged.

Bringing the "jump" to life required a hybrid of [practical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practical_effects "Practical effects") and digital effects.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Fanexpo_Spore_2017-09-10-22) On set, more than 500 individually wired LEDs and a [DMX network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Multiplex "Digital Multiplex") allowed the production team to trigger the teal-and-black [lighting cue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_/(theatrical/)#Cue_lights "Cue (theatrical)") that signals "black alert". [Computer-generated imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery") animators later added the ring-spin and flash in [post-production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-production "Post-production").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Fanexpo_Spore_2017-09-10-22) Graphics lead [Tim Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Peel "Tim Peel") noted that up to twenty layers of practical screens run simultaneously on the bridge so that actors are "really inside the effect," reducing the amount of compositing needed during each jump sequence. Set designer [Matt Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Morgan "Matt Morgan") added that the underslung bridge and surrounding ring forced builders to [raise the entire room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_construction "Set construction") twelve feet above the stage floor, allowing cameras to track the saucer's rotation.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Fanexpo_Spore_2017-09-10-22)

The spore drive was first introduced in _[Star Trek: Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Discovery "Star Trek: Discovery")_'s fourth episode of the first season, "[The Butcher's Knife Cares Not for the Lamb's Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Butcher%27s_Knife_Cares_Not_for_the_Lamb%27s_Cry "The Butcher's Knife Cares Not for the Lamb's Cry")", in 2017. Harberts acknowledged that the writers would need to address why such a powerful propulsion system disappears from later canon, noting that the entire program might be "classified" by Starfleet—which is exactly what happened.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Lovett_Spore_2017-11-19-23)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Orquiola_Spore_2024-10-09-17)

[![Image 5: Cladosporium sphaerospermum, a radiotrophic fungus first described in 1886.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Cladosporium_sphaerospermum_colony.jpg/250px-Cladosporium_sphaerospermum_colony.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cladosporium_sphaerospermum_colony.jpg)

_[Cladosporium sphaerospermum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cladosporium_sphaerospermum "Cladosporium sphaerospermum")_, a [radiotrophic fungus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiotrophic_fungus "Radiotrophic fungus") first described in 1886.

Writing in _[Reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactor_/(magazine/) "Reactor (magazine)")_, Jonathan Alexandratos explores overlaps between the works of both the real-life and fictional Stamets, particularly how mycoremediation concepts are integral to the story mechanics of the mycelial network and factor into the story in several season 2 episodes of _Star Trek: Discovery_.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alexandratos_Spore_2018-02-21-20) Alexandratos also raises the concept of using the mycelium to [terraform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraforming "Terraforming") a planet, which Doug Bonderud similarly highlights in an article for [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") manufacturer [Northrop Grumman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Grumman "Northrop Grumman").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Northrop_Spore_2018-06-11-8) He further discusses the implications of the network [drawing life into itself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saprotrophic_nutrition "Saprotrophic nutrition"), spreading it [elsewhere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore#Dispersal "Spore"), and its potential to heal or repair harm.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alexandratos_Spore_2018-02-21-20) The last is seen in similar real-life sciences, such as [radiotrophic fungus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiotrophic_fungus "Radiotrophic fungus") in the wake of the [Chernobyl disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernobyl_disaster "Chernobyl disaster").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Dadachova_Melanin_2007-24)

[Ethan Siegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethan_Siegel "Ethan Siegel"), an [astrophysicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrophysicist "Astrophysicist") writing for _Forbes_, examined the theoretical plausibility of the spore drive using concepts from modern physics. He proposed that the drive's effect could be explained by invoking a fourth [spatial dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatial_dimension "Spatial dimension")—allowing a ship to leave three-dimensional space, travel a short distance in this higher dimension, and reenter elsewhere nearly instantaneously. He framed this mechanism as analogous to treating "[subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_in_Star_Trek#Subspace "Technology in Star Trek")" in the franchise as a hidden extra dimension, thus giving the spore network a semi-credible scientific analog. However, Siegel was also critical of the series' decision to base such advanced mechanics on a biological mechanism, noting it would have been more plausible had it involved [exotic particles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_particles#Hypothetical_particles "List of particles") or [energy fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force_field_/(physics/) "Force field (physics)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Siegel_Spore_2019-01-15-4)

Evelyn Koch of the [University of Marburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Marburg "University of Marburg") analyzes the spore drive narrative in _Star Trek: Discovery_ as presenting the tardigrade's forced role as a navigator as an ethically troubling form of symbiosis, the effects of Stamets's DNA modification as leading to a [partial upload](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mind_uploading "Mind uploading") of his [consciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consciousness "Consciousness") into the network, and the mycelial network itself as a morally unclassifiable, [alien intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothetical_types_of_biochemistry "Hypothetical types of biochemistry") that resists [human-centered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropocentrism "Anthropocentrism") interpretation.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Koch_Discovery_Spore_2018-3)

[Steven Salzberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Salzberg "Steven Salzberg"), a [computational biologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_biology "Computational biology"), was dismissive of the spore drive concept, calling it "laughably ridiculous" compared to the merely "physically implausible" warp drive.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Salzberg_Spore_2017-10-30-11) Salzberg was also critical of the plotline where Stamets obtained mycelial network navigation abilities from space tardigrade DNA via horizontal gene transfer.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Salzberg_Spore_2017-10-30-11) The likely origin of the tardigrade DNA story, Salzberg theorized, was a controversial 2015 scientific publication that claimed real tardigrades could absorb foreign DNA into themselves, which was disproven afterward in the same journal.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Salzberg_Spore_2017-10-30-11) The tardigrade DNA in question was reported to be only contaminated specimens.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Salzberg_Spore_2017-10-30-11)

[Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") media scholar Karen Pinkus argues that the spore drive embodies a fantasy of ecological redemption, free from the compromises of real-world [energy transitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_transitions "Energy transitions"). She notes that, unlike current [biofuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biofuels "Biofuels"), the spores in Discovery "don't emit any byproducts, harmful or otherwise" and "are not used up in combustion," describing the system as "a nice immersive fantasy" offering escapism from "unbearable realities today."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-LARB_Spore_2017-11-18-15) Pinkus critiques the spore drive as a speculative fuel fantasy that risks reinforcing complacency in the face of [climate crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"). She warns that it may serve as "a narrative of progress" allowing viewers to "defer now, in the present, any radical shifts in how we [produce and consume energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_consumption "Energy consumption")," echoing what she calls "the tyranny of common sense" surrounding [future fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_fuels "Alternative fuels").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-LARB_Spore_2017-11-18-15)

_[Yarrowia lipolytica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarrowia_lipolytica "Yarrowia lipolytica")_, a fungus associated with [necrobiomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrobiome "Necrobiome") and [mycoremediation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycoremediation "Mycoremediation") of decomposing organisms, which Stanway compared to the mycelial network in _Star Trek_. The fictional network recycles matter and creates life, as seen in "Saints of Imperfection" (Discovery S2E5). Dried and heat-killed _Y. lipolytica_ yeast is recognized as a safe [novel food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novel_food "Novel food") by the [European Food Safety Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Food_Safety_Authority "European Food Safety Authority").

Bettina Wurche, in a [ScienceBlogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ScienceBlogs "ScienceBlogs") article on mycology in _Star Trek: Discovery_, compared the Discovery's spore-drive navigator to the mutated Navigators of the [Spacing Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacing_Guild "Spacing Guild") in [Frank Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Herbert "Frank Herbert")'s _[Dune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune_/(franchise/) "Dune (franchise)")_ series, who "\[fold\] space" using the spice [melange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melange_/(Dune/) "Melange (Dune)").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Wurche_Spore_2018-01-03-25) Herbert's 1965 novel describes melange as originating from a "fungusoid wild growth."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Herbert_Spice_Dune_1965-26) Other organic faster-than-light systems depicted in fiction include living ships called Leviathans in the _[Farscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farscape "Farscape")_ franchise and _Star Trek_ creator [Gene Roddenberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Roddenberry "Gene Roddenberry")'s television series _[Andromeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andromeda_/(TV_series/) "Andromeda (TV series)")_, whose "slipstream" drive also required an organic navigator, like the spore drive.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alexandratos_Spore_2018-02-21-20)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Howell_warp_spore_2016-04-27-27)

Lisa Meinecke in _Fighting for the Future: Essays on Star Trek: Discovery_ interprets _Star Trek: Discovery's_ spore drive arc as a critique of liberal humanism, arguing that the series displaces Star Trek's historical emphasis on autonomous individualism with a vision rooted in [posthuman connectivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posthumanism "Posthumanism"). She highlights the shift away from human-centered rationality toward an [ecological pluralism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_ecology "Deep ecology"), in which the mycelial network symbolizes interdependence rather than progress through hierarchy. In this framework, Stamets' fusion with the spore drive marks a narrative break from the franchise's tradition of "[enlightened humanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_humanism "Liberal humanism")," positioning his transformation as a political gesture toward [relational ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics_of_care "Ethics of care").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7)

The [University of Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick "University of Warwick")'s Elizabeth Stanway situates _Star Trek: Discovery_ within a science fiction tradition of depicting collective, sentient ecosystems. She discusses the mycelial-based entities in [Sheri S. Tepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheri_S._Tepper "Sheri S. Tepper")'s _Raising the Stones_ (1990), which develop "as a mycelial network which feeds (initially) on a dead human being," eventually guiding inhabitants on "some instinctual, subconscious level." Stanway notes fears within the story of "the corruption of free will and the threat to their self-determination."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Warwick_Stanway_Spore_2024-12-15-13) She observes that similar ideas of a planetary biological network appear in _[Avatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avatar_/(2009_film/) "Avatar (2009 film)")_ (2009) and its sequel, where characters interact with the biosphere via symbiotic neural connections to the goddess-like entity Eywa.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Warwick_Stanway_Spore_2024-12-15-13) Alexandratos, writing in _Reactor_, frames the mycelial network as a "narrative agent" that is not only alive but capable of both ecological destruction and resurrection, paralleling themes of sentient omniscience. He notes the narrative risk of Stamets becoming "too powerful" through his connection to the network, raising questions about power, agency, and narrative control.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Alexandratos_Spore_2018-02-21-20)

Meinecke identifies Stamets' transformation through the spore drive as an enactment of posthuman becoming, contrasting it with the franchise's prior depiction of android identity in _[Star Trek: The Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Next_Generation "Star Trek: The Next Generation")_. Where [Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_/(Star_Trek/) "Data (Star Trek)") sought to approximate humanness as an ideal, Stamets' evolution rejects autonomy in favor of entanglement with nonhuman life. According to Meinecke, Stamets becomes a "[partial subject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subject_/(philosophy/) "Subject (philosophy)")" in a shared, open-ended network—his identity redefined by affective ties to the tardigrade, his spouse [Hugh Culber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Culber "Hugh Culber"), and the mycelium itself. In doing so, Discovery reframes identity as contingent, collective, and nonhierarchical.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7) _Star Trek: Discovery_ reimagines the [rhizomatic potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhizome_/(philosophy/) "Rhizome (philosophy)") first glimpsed in the [Borg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borg_/(Star_Trek/) "Borg (Star Trek)")—but purges it of authoritarian sameness in favor of posthuman hybridity. According to Meinecke, unlike the Borg collective, which neutralizes difference, the mycelial network fosters egalitarian entanglement and [ethical co-agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agency_/(philosophy/) "Agency (philosophy)"). In this view, Stamets does not merely interface with alien technology—he enters into a reciprocal bond that models a new [ontological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontology "Ontology") vision rooted in sustainability, relationality, and pluralism.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7)

The spore drive is depicted as a "complex [cybernetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybernetics "Cybernetics") multispecies assemblage," with the starship Discovery linked to the mycelial network via the tardigrade interface.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7) This integration allows the ship "access to the [multiplicities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicity_/(philosophy/) "Multiplicity (philosophy)") of possible pathways across the universe, to an infinite number of possible entrances."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7) Stamets' use of the drive initiates a process of "becoming-with the tardigrade and the mycelium," one that is described as "continuous and transformative."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7)

As Stamets becomes "integrated into the drive system," he "steps apart from Discovery and allies himself to the mycelium and the tardigrade." In this "[liminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liminality "Liminality") position between the ship and the network," he gains "the ability to cross these boundaries and gain access to new pathways." Stamets "takes on the tardigrade's position in the drive system and thus the ability to navigate through and thus communicate with the network." His "mind and, in fact, his body are quite literally opened to another [plane of existence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_/(esotericism/) "Plane (esotericism)")." The transformation initially manifests as "a state of somewhat uncharacteristic euphoria and affection towards his friends and colleagues; after all, Stamets just connected to all living things in a profoundly spiritual, transcendent experience (1x07)."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7)

Later, "navigating the regenerating rhizome almost causes him to lose his way," but he stabilizes through his relationship with Culber and the recurring metaphor of the "'clearing in the forest' (1x13)."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7) The mycelial network is explicitly called "a multispecies rhizome, entangling and empowering all life," while the spore drive itself is described as "an extremely powerful [transhumanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transhumanism "Transhumanism") cybernetic [biotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology "Biotechnology") at the interface to this network."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7)

The narrative is framed in ethical terms through comparison to a prior _[Star Trek: Voyager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Voyager "Star Trek: Voyager")_ storyline. The show's use of the tardigrade echoes Voyager's two-part episode "[Equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox_/(Star_Trek:_Voyager/) "Equinox (Star Trek: Voyager)")" (5x26, 6x01), in which another Starfleet crew exploits alien lifeforms to fuel their ship. The authors note that "Saru's decision to employ the tardigrade as navigator is motivated by a similarly existential anxiety." However, they contrast [Saru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saru_/(Star_Trek:_Discovery/) "Saru (Star Trek: Discovery)")'s approach with that of Captain [Kathryn Janeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Janeway "Kathryn Janeway"), who "tries everything in her power to curtail further use of the aliens for fuel" in accordance with Federation ethics.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spore_drive#cite_note-Meinecke_Spore_2020-7)

Why Starfleet Didn't Remake Discovery's Spore Drive In Star Trek: The Original Series & TNG
===========================================================================================

Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents:

Try something different:

Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap

Starfleet did not attempt to remake [_**Star Trek: Discovery**_](https://screenrant.com/db/tv-show/star-trek-discovery/)'s spore drive in _Star Trek: The Original Series_ or _Star Trek: The Next Generation_'s eras. _Star Trek: Discovery_ season 1, which was set in 2256-2257, introduced the displacement-activated spore hub drive, or spore drive, for short. **_Discovery_'s revolutionary spore drive was the series 'big idea,'** which was a significant leap forward as a _Star Trek_ technology. The spore drive allowed the USS Discovery to instantaneously travel through the mycelial network so that the starship essentially teleports to its destination. But why did Starfleet limit the spore drive to the USS Discovery?

[_Star Trek: Discovery_'s spore drive was controversial](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-discovery-spore-drive-how-it-works-why-controversy/) because it was canon-breaking technology far more advanced than anything seen in _Star Trek: The Original Series_, which takes place a decade later. Nor is a spore drive and instantaneous starship teleportation seen in _Star Trek: The Next Generation_'s 24th century era. **_Star Trek: Discovery_ season 2 solved these grievances** by making the spore drive part of an overall crisis surrounding the very existence of the USS Discovery. After Discovery merged with a 100,000-year-old sphere and its data was uploaded into Disco's computers, the starship became the target of a rogue A.I. called Control. With the sphere data, Control could become fully sentient and wipe out all organic life in the galaxy.

Discovery's Spore Drive Technology Was A Closely-Guarded Secret Within Starfleet
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The USS Discovery and the spore drive were redacted

At the [end of _Star Trek: Discovery_ season 2](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-discovery-season-2-ending-future-explained/), the combined forces of the USS Discovery, the USS Enterprise, and their allies, including the Kelpiens, destroyed Control, Section 31's genocidal threat assessment A.I. However, in order to prevent another Control from becoming online and sentient, Discovery, its sphere data, and its spore drive had to be removed from the 23rd century. To safeguard the galaxy, Commander Michael Burnham (Sonequa Martin-Green) led the USS Discovery on a permanent, one-way trip 930 years into the 32nd century. In the real world, this was also **_Star Trek: Discovery'_s solution to the problem of the starship being too technologically advanced for _Star Trek'_s 23rd century**. In the distant future, Discovery could set _Star Trek_ canon instead of defy it.

Knowledge of the USS Discovery and its spore drive was simply forgotten by the 24th century.

Once the USS Discovery was no longer in the 23rd century, [Captain Christopher Pike](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-strange-new-worlds-captain-pike-missing-arch-enemy/) (Anson Mount) and Lieutenant Spock (Ethan Peck) of the USS Enterprise reported to Starfleet that Discovery was destroyed and all hands lost. Further, Spock redacted the USS Discovery from Starfleet records to protect Michael Burnham, his adopted sister. **The USS Discovery's spore drive technology was redacted** along with the starship's records so that Starfleet could not build another. As time passed, and Starfleet continued to rely on standard warp drive, knowledge of the USS Discovery and its spore drive was simply forgotten by the 24th century.

Starfleet Knew The Spore Drive Was Almost Impossible To Use In Practice
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### A spore drive needs a navigator

The USS Discovery's spore displacement hub drive was also dangerous technology that **required a specialized navigator for it to work.** In [_Star Trek: Discovery_ season 1](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-discovery-season-1-every-good-thing/), two Crossfield Class starships experimented with spore drive technology. The USS Glenn attempted a spore drive jump through the mycelial network that killed everyone aboard. However, the Glenn had a giant tardigrade that was brought aboard the USS Discovery, and the crew soon deduced that the tardigrade, named Ripper, could serve as the spore drive's navigator. Unfortunately, the tardigrade was debilitated by interfacing with the spore drive, so Discovery's crew released it back into space.

[Lieutenant Paul Stamets (Anthony Rapp)](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-discovery-anthony-rapp-paul-stamets-explained/) injected himself with tardigrade DNA and augmented himself to become the USS Discovery's spore drive navigator. In _Star Trek: Discovery_ season 3, Cleveland Booker (David Ajala) learned his Kwejian DNA and empathic abilities also let him serve as the spore drive's navigator. However, **the genetic manipulation Stamets underwent is illegal in the United Federation of Planets**. Since tardigrade DNA was a requirement to safely interface with the spore drive, it was logical for Starfleet to abandon the technology, which would be impossible to replicate on other starships.

Any Spore Drive Research Would've Been Quashed By Starfleet
-----------------------------------------------------------

### Section 31 doesn't want another Control to be created

Even if Starfleet scientists had access to the USS Discovery's redacted files, Starfleet and Section 31 would never allow new research into spore drive technology. The combined tragedies of the USS Glenn and the USS Discovery are enough to keep Starfleet from pursuing the creation of another spore drive. In addition, Control was Section 31's A.I. and the black ops organization would have prevented any attempt to create a spore drive that could somehow lead to another Control being built. Ultimately, **the concept of starships instantly teleporting was abandoned** in favor of Starfleet finding new ways to make standard warp travel faster.

Starfleet also knew the USS Discovery's spore drive was used to jump to and from the Mirror Universe, which is another danger that justified banning spore drives.

Instead of new spore drive or starship teleportation technology**,** [improving warp drives](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-warp-drive-new-versions-starfleet/) became Starfleet's goal. In _Star Trek III: The Search For Spock_, the USS Excelsior was built with _"the Great Experiment,"_ a transwarp drive. Unfortunately, after it was sabotaged by Scotty (James Doohan), Starfleet also mothballed the transwarp drive. Trapped in the Delta Quadrant, the USS Voyager developed quantum slipsteam technology to accelerate its journey home in _Star Trek: Voyager_. **_Star Trek: Prodigy_ introduced the Proto Drive**, which harnesses the power of a baby star to make the USS Protostar the fastest starship of its time.

Star Trek's 32nd Century Also Abandoned Discovery's Spore Drive
---------------------------------------------------------------

### Starfleet chose to adopt the Pathway Drive

Ironically, Starfleet in the 32nd century also chose to abandon spore drive technology. Even though the USS Discovery was almost a thousand years old when it arrived in 3189, Starfleet had no technology that could equal Discovery's spore drive. In fact, the Federation was broken and isolated for nearly a century after a calamity called [the Burn wiped out dilithium crystals in starships](https://screenrant.com/star-trek-discovery-the-burn-mystery-solution-explained/) and eliminated warp travel. With its ability to teleport using the spore drive, as well as a functional standard warp drive, the **USS Discovery became the lynchpin of 32nd century Starfleet** and its primary weapon to diffuse crises threatening the Federation.
