15.content:
The idea of “mycelial networks” is so buzzy right now. Folks throw around the phrase to illustrate everything from a cooperative vibe in a conference room to Buddhist ideas of interconnectedness with nature and her inherent wisdom, but frankly, I find it kind of annoying that the metaphor has drifted so far away from the mycology. Because from what I can tell, there’s a lot of confusion about just what a mycelial connection is (and isn’t).

I recently published an essay on this subject in _[Revista de la Universidad de México](https://www.revistadelauniversidad.mx/releases/6745a934-bfe8-418e-9d72-db25749a4457/redes),_ a National Autonomous University of Mexico's cultural magazine, translated by Pablo Duarte. The piece is beautifully illustrated with images of work by [Rodrigo Arteaga Abarca](https://www.rodrigoarteaga.com/). I rarely write for magazines anymore, so this was really a pleasure.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0yVy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6902ce8b-ce5d-4c16-a081-c0f4eae3f91e_478x700.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0yVy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6902ce8b-ce5d-4c16-a081-c0f4eae3f91e_478x700.jpeg)

Here’s how it came about: the editors of the magazine had reached out saying they were planning an issue around networks, and wanted to know if I would be interested in writing about mycelium. At first I was afraid they, like so many others, were smitten with the notion of the “mycelial connection,” and would want some kind of Hallmark version of nature where only good things happen, but if they were, they were quick to let it go and embrace my opinion that the metaphor becomes more potent if you understand a little mycology.

So for those of you who don’t read Spanish, below is the English original. (I don’t recommend selecting “translate” if you open the magazine—that’s a game of telephone run amok.)

**It used to be** when I went to a dinner party and I’d tell my dining companion I was into mushrooms and molds, inevitably they’d start looking for somewhere else to sit. But not anymore. I just published a book about magic mushrooms (it’s called _Have a Good Trip_) and now _I_ am the one looking for somewhere else to sit, otherwise I’m trapped answering a bazillion questions about _Psilocybe_ mushrooms, and mushrooms more generally.

Interest in fungi has swelled; mushrooms are the newest health and wellness trend. The mushroom clubs, once the domain of retired hobbyists, a few cranks, and the occasional quirky child, are now populated with folks making careers in cultivation, education, product manufacture, and guiding, both in the woods and, for those into magic mushrooms, in the mind. These days I’m drowning in internet alerts about mushroom forays, recipes, cures, fashion, art, music, and design from serious to kitsch, mushroom environmental remediation, new product development and engineering, and fungi’s impact on agriculture. But most of all, I’ve noticed that the hackneyed use of the term mycelium, which refers to the feeding structure of certain fungal species, has become virtually synonymous with the healing powers of helping each other.

This last notion derives from mostly 21st century research showing that the forest is not just a collection of trees, but a community connected underground by one or more fungal mycelia that sustain balance and well-being in the ecosystem.[\[1\]](https://eugeniabone.substack.com/p/mycelium-mycology-and-metaphor?utm_source=%2Fbrowse%2Fscience&utm_medium=reader2#_ftn1) This new understanding of forest ecosystems has proliferated through movies like _Avatar_ and _Fantastic Fungi_ which gave fungi voice and intention, thanks to actress Brie Larson; books like _[The Secret Life of Trees](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-whispering-trees-180968084/)_ and television shows like _Star Trek: [Discovery](https://memory-alpha.fandom.com/wiki/Mycelial_network)_ which developed a plot line in its first season about the mycelial network, “a vast microscopic web…that spans the multiverse.” Countless podcasts, businesses, and seminars applaud the wonders of the “mycelial connection,” even promoting the idea of a “[Human Mycelium](https://www.theoctopusmovement.org/post/the-human-mycelium-connecting-our-sense-of-self-and-solving-global-problems#:~:text=The%20concept%20of%20the%20Human,nutrients%20and%20supporting%20the%20ecosystem)” which “draws an analogy between the mycelial networks formed by fungi and the interconnectedness of human beings.” The relationship between trees and certain fungi seems to have morphed beyond the boundaries of their biology and become a symbol of the inherent goodness of interdependent relationships. Too bad that’s a very narrow understanding of the mycology.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E8wT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F957b0c98-8ae9-45ba-b5ed-b2366ccb28d3_1920x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E8wT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F957b0c98-8ae9-45ba-b5ed-b2366ccb28d3_1920x1080.jpeg)

_Still from the movie Avatar dir. James Cameron (2009)_

But I have an idea of why it’s happening. As more and more people (in the USA anyway) experience how divisive and scary our world is today, metaphors about the innate goodness of fungi can bring a sense of hope and promise that _our_ better natures will prevail.

I am not interested in degrading that sentiment—I’d prefer our better natures prevail, too--but I think when sentiment replaces science, it distracts us from a deeper appreciation of the complexity of nature, and that could inhibit actual ecological cooperation. I’m not alone in this thinking. In their [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-023-01986-1.epdf?sharing_token=4rV4cFsIJsGwjzRZb6RB5tRgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0NhTP-fzuHqUsVVnDaJbaXlPDeSXUxYqcTbqUWYB-bJgn5sJ5o-vFQAc1fe91Wjq81-yXT7qIcdNnXZu0UK67aDXrgd1oiX3ZWXdHC51uCa3Quw83xPDyU_jYc5PflgVtnyTKhJrYRNr5WgP5dKfC-9KqCGDJtmOQKOg8CBUKnE_ZB6CFySXeSphwDF5Xb1Eow%3D&tracking_referrer=www.scientificamerican.com) “Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests,” the authors point out that while they are “thrilled that the public has become as excited as we are about the many roles that fungi play in forests…\[n\]onetheless, it is important for the public and scientific community to understand the nature and extent of the evidence for the roles played by common mycorrhizal networks in forests.”

So for those who are in love with the idea of the mycelial network, here’s a quick overview of what is known about these amazing organisms. Of the many fungal species, some are single celled, like yeasts, and others are multicellular, like molds and the species that produce mushrooms. The multicellular form of a fungus is called the mycelium (plus there are other multicellular structures that occur, like sclerotia or rhizomorphs but we are not talking about those today). A mycelium is a web of microscopic tubes that seeks and consumes food. It contains a fungus’ genetic info, it can regenerate when torn apart as it has no front or back, and it can fuse with other, compatible mycelia.

A mycelium grows from a spore, which is like a tiny, light seed that contains only a little bit of energy. When an airborne spore lands on the food it likes to eat it has just enough energy to germinate. That’s why it is so important a spore lands on its food—so it can start consuming right away (and that’s also why a fungus, however it does so, launches many, many spores into its environment; to increase the chances that a spore will land on something edible).

Fungi are too small to have stomachs, so they digest food _outside_ their bodies. If you were a fungal spore and you landed on your preferred food, say, a strawberry, you would seep out your digestive juices, break down the strawberry flesh, and absorb the nutrients, like water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sugar, and then you’d have the energy to grow a little bigger, one cell at a time into long tube-like threads called hyphae. As the hyphae grow, they branch and rebranch, each tip an absorption point that explores their environment for food and in some cases, for symbiotic partners. (This [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08614-x) shares some very interesting new science on the growth pattern of mycelia.) This mass of hyphal threads is called a mycelium. A mycelium can grow in any dimension or direction there is food to grow into, which is why the mycelium of a fungus like ring worm is only skin deep. _Tinea corporis_ consumes keratin in skin, not tissue. It doesn’t grow where there isn’t food.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EYRm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9bf66e92-d4cf-4568-972a-35858b8a3546_2400x1350.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EYRm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9bf66e92-d4cf-4568-972a-35858b8a3546_2400x1350.jpeg)

_Creator: reanas | Credit: Getty Images/iStockphoto Copyright: reanas_

Since fungi are absorptive organisms, one way to describe the way they live is by what they eat. Fungi don’t make the carbon they need so they must get it from elsewhere. Parasitic fungi—mostly blights and rots of plants--get their carbon by predation: they kill their prey and consume the prey’s carbon. Saprobic fungi get their carbon by eating dead and dying stuff, mainly plants. When you kick open a rotting log, that fluffy white stuff is the mycelium of saprobic fungi which is busy consuming the wood’s nutrients. Mutualists, which include endophytic fungi and mycorrhizal fungi, get their carbon through trade with a living plant.

It's the mycorrhizal fungi that people are referring to when they speak of the mycelium network—whether they know it or not. But it’s helpful to know, I think, that a mycelium is the thallus--an undifferentiated body--of many multicellular fungi including parasites. Which means the “mycelial network” metaphor is less about the mycelium and more about how particular mycelia get their food.

It has long been established that most plants—70 to 90%--participate in mutualistic relationships with fungi. It has been described as a trade: part of the fungus attaches to the root tips of the plant. The rest forages in the soil and delivers micronutrients in a readily assimilated form that the plant needs, like phosphorus, but can’t make. In exchange or trade, the plant shares with the fungus sugars it makes by means of photosynthesis.

But what bumped mycorrhizae into the realm of metaphor started with the work of Dr. Suzanne Simard from the University of British Columbia. Simard discovered that fungi attach to the roots of multiple trees in a particular ecosystem, in essence creating nutritional pipelines from which the trees might benefit, and in the process defining a particular forest community. As she wrote in her book, _Finding the Mother Tree_, this cooperation “challenge\[s\] the prevailing theory that cooperation is of less importance than competition in evolution and ecology.”

Simard and her colleagues proved this with a simple, well-crafted field experiment: she labeled tree sugars with radioactive isotopes and then tracked them as they traveled through fungal hyphae into the root tips of other trees. Her [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/41557) was published in _Nature_ in 1996, and it made the cover, beating out the discovery of the fruit fly genome (more important than it sounds). The editors of _Nature_ came up with the title “The Wood Wide Web” and today it’s shorthand for more than the networks of trees and their fungal symbionts in a given ecosystem; it has become what Richard Power’s calls in _The Overstory_ “The Gospel of New Forestry” (the character Patricia Westerfield is based on Simard) and a metaphor for cooperation as a means to success and happiness.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A8YZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a2d7312-2e3e-48a9-bd25-111b3bbe8c0d_1400x1052.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A8YZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a2d7312-2e3e-48a9-bd25-111b3bbe8c0d_1400x1052.png)

Suzanne’s work suggests that through fungal networks trees share resources, and mature trees (what she calls “hub trees” in her research and “mother trees” when speaking to popular audiences) support seedlings, favor their kin, and distribute resources, even in death. Weaker plants will tap into this network, like crashers at an all-you-can-eat buffet. Young seedlings struggling to grow in the shadow of a canopy may tap into the larger, older tree’s fungal network to supplement their nutrition. This network benefits not only established trees and seedlings of the same species, but also trees from different species, and at different stages of development. So one multitasking fungus, its hyphae attached to the roots of multiple trees in the forest, can simultaneously provide a different nutritional load as needed to different trees. “In one forest we found 47 trees linked by two species of fungi composed of twelve individuals,” said Simard. (When she says individuals, she means two genetically distinct fungal entities.) “Talk about two degrees of separation!”

Nor is Simard the only scientist to pursue this radical new understanding of plants and their mycorrhizal connections. A 2013 [study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/ele.12115) by scientists at the University of Aberdeen found that bean plants connected to one another by mycorrhizal fungi can convey chemical “warnings” of an impending attack through the fungal hyphae they share.

The mutualistic nature of the plant/fungus relationship is what fuels people’s enthusiasm about the so-called mycelium network. But that’s not the whole picture. Fungi may provide environmental services to plants in an ecosystem, but they also may deny those services. It depends on what’s in their own best interest.

For example, a [paper](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2420701122) that came out in PNAS in late January titled “Evolution of signaling and monitoring in plant-fungal networks” suggests that the mycorrhizal fungus probably doesn’t help plants because it’s a good thing to do, but rather when a fungus that connects two plants detects an aphid attack and signals the other plants in the network, it does so because it is evolutionarily beneficial for the fungus to have multiple symbiotic partners.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rl0N!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe664bd21-9ddb-498c-87f2-9bcb10f414dd_950x730.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rl0N!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe664bd21-9ddb-498c-87f2-9bcb10f414dd_950x730.png)

Illustration from **The evolution of signaling and monitoring in plant–fungal networks**

Mutualism is ultimately about commonly shared self-interest. In forest ecosystems, fungal networks may determine which plants need its foraged nutrients the most, and which plants have the most carbon to offer. Fungi don’t partner up with just any plant; sometimes they prefer partnerships with plants some distance away because the carbon payoff is [greater.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08614-x) “The fungus is basically a microbe that plays economic games,” said Tom Shimizu a biophysicist at AMOLF, a physics institute in Amsterdam in a _New York Times_ [article.](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/01/science/climate-mycorrhizal-fungus-networks.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share&referringSource=articleShare&sgrp=p&pvid=D64C88E9-6D02-40B8-8951-AEAEB40FEC7D) The flows of carbon in fungal hyphae, according to evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers of the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks, are under fungal control. But how the fungus moves these nutrients around is unknown, as is how a noncognitive organism like a fungus makes decisions.

The late mycologist Tom Volk used to describe the plant-fungus symbiosis as a hostage situation, where the fungus holds back nutrients to the tree unless it delivers the sugar. That’s quite different from Suzanne Simard’s sympathetic interpretation of the plant/fungus relationship.

It seems to me that the “mycelium network” metaphor is based on two cherry-picked ideas. The first is that mycelium is by nature a magnanimous organism. It is not. It is the thallus of multicellular fungi, some of which are parasites, some saprobes, some mycorrhizae. Mycelium has become a stand in word for a mycorrhizal fungus and its role in a forest ecosystem.

The second cherry-picked idea is that mycorrhizal fungi play an altruistic role in the environment. You can look at that role as being beneficent, but there’s no proof of that characterization. Indeed, there may be more evidence supporting the idea that mycorrhizal fungi function based on self-interest.

Characterizing mycelium as generous nurturers of forest ecosystems is a kind of anthropomorphism, where we have attributed human characteristics to fungi. Anthropomorphism is an established [tool](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/209660831900200103S) of science communication. It’s used to help people who don’t understand a science feel connected to it. And certainly not a lot of people know much about mycology. For most of academic history, mushrooms were studied (to the extent they were studied at all) within university botany departments. Traditionally, botanists lumped fungi together with plants when in fact, fungi constitute a huge, unique taxonomic rank representing a wide range of lifestyles and morphologies.

But unless you take graduate level biology, a student’s exposure to fungi may be scant. I went back to my old university, Columbia in New York, to study undergrad biology for a year and we had one lecture on fungi. One.

When someone who lacks a background in basic mycology first learns about fungi--their ubiquity, their diversity, their crucial roles in ecologies as diverse as the atmosphere and your skin, and in some cases their bioactive compounds--mushrooms can seem utterly miraculous. I know for myself when I first started getting into mycology, I was dazzled to learn of a whole kingdom of life of which I knew nothing. It was like finding out ghosts are real.

But that intellectual vulnerability has, in my view, enabled people to believe hypothetical, even fictionalized characterizations of the role of fungi in nature and in particular, the notion that mycelium is selfless, compassionate, and generous; all qualities that we need more of in our world right now. But in fact, from the fungal point of view, life is as much about opportunism as collaboration.

We love a story because it makes us feel good and it helps us relate. But let’s not confuse metaphor with mycology. Because inspirational as metaphor may be, it doesn’t solve real world problems like forest and soil degradation, carbon release, and mineral-deficient crops.

But mycology can.

[\[1\]](https://eugeniabone.substack.com/p/mycelium-mycology-and-metaphor?utm_source=%2Fbrowse%2Fscience&utm_medium=reader2#_ftnref1) The idea of mutual reciprocity in nature has all kinds of provenance, including the Gaia Hypothesis by futurist James Lovelock. It described earth as a “series of interacting ecosystems that compose a single huge ecosystem at the Earth’s surface.” _Lovelock J (1979) Gaia: A New Look at Life on Earth Oxford University Press_ The hypothesis animated some of the New Age thinking of the Baby Boomer generation which in turn has fathered much of the hoopla about the “mycelial network.”

13.content:
**Directed panspermia** is a type of [panspermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panspermia "Panspermia") that implies the deliberate transport of microorganisms into space to be used as [introduced species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introduced_species "Introduced species") on other [astronomical objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_object "Astronomical object").

Shklovskii and Sagan (1966) and Crick and Orgel (1973) hypothesized that [life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life "Life") on the Earth may have been seeded deliberately by other civilizations. Conversely, Mautner and Matloff (1979) and [Mautner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_N._Mautner "Michael N. Mautner") (1995, 1997) proposed that humanity should seed other planetary systems, [protoplanetary discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protoplanetary_disc "Protoplanetary disc") or star-forming clouds with [microorganisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microorganism "Microorganism"). Motivations for directed panspermia often stem from panbiotic ethics[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner2-1) and as a last resort existential risk mitigation strategy.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-2) However, more recently directed panspermia has also been heavily criticised from the perspectives of contamination and interference with indigenous life,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-:0-3) wild animal welfare concerns,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-:1-4)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-:0-3) and procreative ethics,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-:1-4) highlighting in particular, concerns about its irreversibility in the context of its uncertain ethical consequences.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-5)

Directed panspermia is becoming possible due to developments in [solar sails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_sails "Solar sails"), precise [astrometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrometry "Astrometry"), the discovery of [extrasolar planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrasolar_planets "Extrasolar planets"), [extremophiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremophiles "Extremophiles") and microbial [genetic engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_engineering "Genetic engineering").

History and motivation
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and motivation")\]

An early example of the idea of directed panspermia dates to the early [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") work _[Last and First Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_and_First_Men "Last and First Men")_ by [Olaf Stapledon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olaf_Stapledon "Olaf Stapledon"), first published in 1930. It details the manner in which the last humans, upon discovering that the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") will soon be destroyed, send microscopic "seeds of a new humanity" towards potentially [habitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_habitability "Planetary habitability") areas of the universe.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-6)

In 1966, [Shklovskii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iosif_Shklovsky "Iosif Shklovsky") and [Sagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sagan "Carl Sagan") speculated that life on Earth may have been seeded through directed panspermia by other civilisations,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-7) and, in 1973, Crick and Orgel also discussed the concept.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-8) In the controversial 2008 documentary _[Expelled: No Intelligence Allowed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expelled:_No_Intelligence_Allowed "Expelled: No Intelligence Allowed")_ starring [Ben Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Stein "Ben Stein"), [Richard Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dawkins "Richard Dawkins") mentioned directed panspermia as a possible scenario and that scientists may find evidence of it hidden in human biological chemistry and [molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-9) Conversely, Mautner and Matloff proposed in 1979, and Mautner examined in detail in 1995 and 1997 the technology and motivation to secure and expand organic gene/protein life-form by directed panspermia missions to other planetary systems, [protoplanetary discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protoplanetary_disc "Protoplanetary disc") and star-forming clouds.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-SeedingBook-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner1-11)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner2-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12) Technological aspects include propulsion by solar sails, deceleration by [radiation pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation_pressure "Radiation pressure") or viscous drag at the target, and capture of the colonizing micro-organisms by planets. A possible objection is potential interference with local life at the targets, but targeting young planetary systems where local life, especially advanced life, could not have started yet, avoids this problem.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12)

Directed panspermia may be motivated by the desire to perpetuate the common genetic heritage of all terrestrial life. This motivation was formulated as biotic ethics that value the common gene/protein patterns of self propagation,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner4-13) and as panbiotic ethics that aim to secure and expand life in the universe.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner2-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12)

Strategies and targets
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Strategies and targets")\]

Directed panspermia may be aimed at nearby young planetary systems such as Alpha PsA (25 ly ([light-years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-year "Light-year")) away) and [Beta Pictoris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Pictoris "Beta Pictoris") (63.4 ly), both of which show [accretion discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accretion_disc "Accretion disc") and signs of comets and planets. More suitable targets may be identified by space telescopes such as the [Kepler mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_mission "Kepler mission") that will identify nearby star systems with habitable [astronomical objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_object "Astronomical object"). Alternatively, directed panspermia may aim at star-forming interstellar clouds such as [Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rho_Ophiuchi_cloud_complex "Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex") (427 ly), that contains clusters of new stars too young to originate local life (425 infrared-emitting young stars aged 100,000 to a million years). Such clouds contain zones with various densities (diffuse cloud < dark fragment < dense core < protostellar condensation < accretion disc)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-14) that could selectively capture panspermia capsules of various sizes.

Habitable astronomical objects or habitable zones about nearby stars may be targeted by large (10 kg) missions where microbial capsules are bundled and shielded. Upon arrival, microbial capsules in the payload may be dispersed in orbit for capture by planets. Alternatively, small microbial capsules may be sent in large swarms to habitable planets, [protoplanetary discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protoplanetary_discs "Protoplanetary discs"), or zones of various density in interstellar clouds. The microbial swarm provides minimal shielding but does not require high precision targeting, especially when aiming at large interstellar clouds.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-SeedingBook-10)

Propulsion and launch
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Propulsion and launch")\]

Panspermia missions should deliver microorganisms that can grow in the new habitats. They may be sent in 10−10 kg, 60 μm diameter capsules that allow intact atmospheric entry at the target planets, each containing 100,000 diverse microorganisms suited to various environments. Both for bundled large mass missions and microbial capsule swarms, [solar sails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_sails "Solar sails") may provide the most simple propulsion for interstellar transit.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-15) Spherical sails will avoid orientation control both at launch and at deceleration at the targets.

For bundled shielded missions to nearby star systems, [solar sails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_sail "Solar sail") with thicknesses of 10−7 m and areal densities of 0.0001 kg/m2 seem feasible, and sail/payload mass ratios of 10:1 will allow exit velocities near the maximum possible for such sails. Sails with about 540 m radius and area of 106 m2 can impart 10 kg payloads with interstellar cruise velocities of 0.0005 _c_ (1.5×105 m/s) when launched from 1 au (astronomical unit). At this speed, voyage to the Alpha PsA star will last 50,000 y, and to the Rho Opiuchus cloud, 824,000 years.

At the targets, the microbial payload would decompose into 1011 (100 billion) 30 μm capsules to increase the probability of capture. In the swarm strategy to protoplanetary discs and interstellar clouds, 1 mm radius, 4.2×10−6 kg microbial capsules are launched from 1 au using sails of 4.2×10−5 kg with radius of 0.37 m and area of 0.42 m2 to achieve cruising speeds of 0.0005 _[c](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light "Speed of light")_. At the target, each capsule decomposes into 4,000 delivery microcapsules of 10−10 kg and of 30 micrometer radius that allow intact entry to planetary atmospheres.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Anders-16)

For missions that do not encounter dense gas zones, such as interstellar transit to mature planets or to habitable zones about stars, the microcapsules can be launched directly from 1 au using 10−9 kg sails of 1.8 mm radius to achieve velocities of 0.0005 _c_ to be decelerated by [radiation pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation_pressure "Radiation pressure") for capture at the targets. The 1 mm and 30 micrometer radius vehicles and payloads are needed in large numbers for both the bundled and swarm missions. These capsules and the miniature sails for swarm missions can be mass manufactured readily.

Astrometry and targeting
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Astrometry and targeting")\]

The panspermia vehicles would be aimed at moving targets whose locations at the time of arrival must be predicted. This can be calculated using their measured proper motions, their distances, and the cruising speeds of the vehicles. The positional uncertainty and size of the target object then allow estimating the probability that the panspermia vehicles will arrive at their targets. The positional uncertainty ![Image 1: {\displaystyle \delta y}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1dc454b7f0e03259e9c5e8568fcef1c8e6b78230) (m) of the target at arrival time is given by the following equation, where ![Image 2: {\displaystyle \alpha _{p}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5c48aa9000af59f94d3022f58beadb61cea7d8b5) is the resolution of proper motion of the target object (arcsec/year), ![Image 3: {\displaystyle d}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e85ff03cbe0c7341af6b982e47e9f90d235c66ab)d is the distance from the Earth (m) and ![Image 4: {\displaystyle v}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e07b00e7fc0847fbd16391c778d65bc25c452597) is the velocity of the vehicle (m s−1).[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12)

![Image 5: {\displaystyle \delta y={\frac {1.5\times 10^{-13}\alpha _{p}d^{2}}{v}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2ede8c6eca02585c42f97f6691da6589419eacb5)

Given the positional uncertainty, the vehicles may be launched with a scatter in a circle about the predicted position of the target. The probability ![Image 6: {\displaystyle P_{\text{target}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0cd11817e430331c5d2c999202fa9dcddcb57b89) for a capsule to hit the target area with radius ![Image 7: {\displaystyle r_{\text{target}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1aeb161fe9f1304ef906caa9c873fd8ca6d2df2c) (m) is given by the ratio of the targeting scatter and the target area.

![Image 8: {\displaystyle P_{\text{target}}={\frac {A_{\text{target}}}{\pi (\delta y)^{2}}}={\frac {4.4\times 10^{25}{r_{\text{target}}}^{2}v^{2}}{{\alpha _{p}}^{2}d^{4}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0a3b35a05a054026ea7fefaa0bcc72d944361a4d)

To apply these equations, the precision of astrometry of star proper motion of 0.00001 arcsec/year, and the solar sail vehicle velocity of 0.0005 [_c_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light "Speed of light") (1.5 × 105 m s−1) may be expected within a few decades. For a chosen planetary system, the area ![Image 9: {\displaystyle A_{\text{target}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0f28722868c62fb89ba4a3e95aa61acd8df6fada) may be the width of the [habitable zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitable_zone "Habitable zone"), while for interstellar clouds, it may be the sizes of the various density zones of the cloud.

Deceleration and capture
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Deceleration and capture")\]

Solar sail missions to Sun-like stars can decelerate by [radiation pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation_pressure "Radiation pressure") in reverse dynamics of the launch. The sails must be properly oriented at arrival, but orientation control may be avoided using spherical sails. The vehicles must approach the target Sun-like stars at radial distances similar to the launch, about 1 au. After the vehicles are captured in orbit, the microbial capsules may be dispersed in a ring orbiting the star, some within the gravitational capture zone of planets. Missions to accretion discs of planets and to star-forming clouds will decelerate by viscous drag at the rate ![Image 10: {\displaystyle {\frac {dv}{dt}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/8e20b178c1895c793f8e906575cd7f2f537b17cc) as determined by the following equation, where ![Image 11: {\displaystyle v}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e07b00e7fc0847fbd16391c778d65bc25c452597) is the velocity, ![Image 12: {\displaystyle r_{c}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5e41dc9dcda9fd0c224d94555361f02b73aacd2e) the radius of the spherical capsule, ![Image 13: {\displaystyle \rho _{c}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/523e8c709cfeaef7ed497ce5be80144fdf2e9b70) is density of the capsule and ![Image 14: {\displaystyle \rho _{m}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fb8e01f5f9a1ec7641573c415df8bfa942a42a78) is the density of the medium.

![Image 15: {\displaystyle {\frac {dv}{dt}}=-{\frac {3v^{2}}{2\rho _{c}}}{\frac {\rho _{m}}{r_{c}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d787ad86e7197c66a4ccd38baaa877784695899b)

A vehicle entering the cloud with a velocity of 0.0005 _c_ (1.5 × 105 m s−1) will be captured when decelerated to 2,000 m s−1, the typical speed of grains in the cloud. The size of the capsules can be designed to stop at zones with various densities in the interstellar cloud. Simulations show that a 35 [μm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron "Micron") radius capsule will be captured in a dense core, and a 1 mm radius capsule in a protostellar condensation in the cloud. As for approach to accretion discs about stars, a millimetre size capsule entering the 1000 km thick disc face at 0.0005 _c_ will be captured at 100 km into the disc. Therefore, 1 mm sized objects may be the best for seeding [protoplanetary discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protoplanetary_discs "Protoplanetary discs") about new stars and protostellar condensations in interstellar clouds.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12)

The captured panspermia capsules will mix with dust. A fraction of the dust and a proportional fraction of the captured capsules will be delivered to astronomical objects. Dispersing the payload into delivery microcapsules will increase the chance that some will be delivered to habitable objects. Particles of 0.6 – 60 μm radius can remain cold enough to preserve organic matter during atmospheric entry to planets or moons.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Anders-16) Accordingly, each 1 mm, 4.2 × 10−6 kg capsule captured in the viscous medium can be dispersed into 42,000 delivery microcapsules of 30 μm radius, each weighing 10−10 kg and containing 100,000 microbes. These objects will not be ejected from the dust cloud by radiation pressure from the star, and will remain mixed with the dust.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-18) A fraction of the dust, containing the captured microbial capsules, will be captured by planets or moons, or captured in comets and delivered by them later to planets. The probability of capture, ![Image 16: {\displaystyle P_{\text{capture}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86451d6879d47b7c90a16e0c3e4e1781e393360f), can be estimated from similar processes, such as the capture of interplanetary dust particles by planets and moons in the Solar System, where 10−5 of the Zodiacal cloud maintained by comet ablation, and also a similar fraction of asteroid fragments, is collected by the Earth.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-20) The probability of capture of an initially launched capsule by a planet (or astronomical object) ![Image 17: {\displaystyle P_{\text{planet}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/6f25ba2c0fa1007d40c1f51a1ed6adeddb428ddd) is given by the equation below, where ![Image 18: {\displaystyle P_{\text{target}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0cd11817e430331c5d2c999202fa9dcddcb57b89) is the probability that the capsule reaches the target accretion disc or cloud zone, and ![Image 19: {\displaystyle P_{\text{capture}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86451d6879d47b7c90a16e0c3e4e1781e393360f) is the probability of capture from this zone by a planet.

![Image 20: {\displaystyle P_{\text{planet}}=P_{\text{target}}\times P_{\text{capture}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7d21f6b0ecdc308950f1ceb4d45d15bc6da780da)

The probability ![Image 21: {\displaystyle P_{\text{planet}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/6f25ba2c0fa1007d40c1f51a1ed6adeddb428ddd) depends on the mixing ratio of the capsules with the dust and on the fraction of the dust delivered to planets. These variables can be estimated for capture in planetary accretion discs or in various zones in the interstellar cloud.

Biomass requirements
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Biomass requirements")\]

After determining the composition of chosen [meteorites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorite "Meteorite"), [astroecologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astroecology "Astroecology") performed laboratory experiments that suggest that many colonizing microorganisms and some plants could obtain most of their chemical nutrients from [asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid") and [cometary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comet "Comet") materials.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-bioresources-21) However, the scientists noted that phosphate (PO4) and [nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate "Nitrate") (NO3–N) critically limit nutrition to many terrestrial lifeforms.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-bioresources-21) For successful missions, enough [biomass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomass "Biomass") must be launched and captured for a reasonable chance to initiate life at the target astronomical object. An optimistic requirement is the capture by the planet of 100 capsules with 100,000 microorganisms each, for a total of 10 million organisms with a total biomass of 10−8 kg.

The required biomass to launch for a successful mission is given by following equation. mbiomass (kg) = 10−8 / Pplanet Using the above equations for Ptarget with transit velocities of 0.0005 c, the known distances to the targets, and the masses of the dust in the target regions then allows calculating the biomass that needs to be launched for probable success. With these parameters, as little as 1 gram of biomass (1012 microorganisms) could seed Alpha PsA and 4.5 gram could seed Beta Pictoris. More biomass needs to be launched to the [Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rho_Ophiuchi_cloud_complex "Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex"), mainly because of its larger distance. A biomass on the order of 300 tons would need to be launched to seed a protostellar condensation or an accretion disc, but two hundred kilograms would be sufficient to seed a young stellar object in the [Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rho_Ophiuchi_cloud_complex "Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex").

Consequently, as long as the required [physical range of tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life#Range_of_tolerance "Life") are met (e.g.: growth temperature, cosmic radiation shielding, atmosphere and gravity), lifeforms viable on Earth may be chemically nourished by watery asteroid and planetary materials in this and other planetary systems.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-bioresources-21)

The seeding organisms need to survive and multiply in the target environments and establish a viable [biosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosphere "Biosphere"). Some of the new branches of life may develop intelligent beings who will further expand life in the galaxy. The messenger microorganisms may find diverse environments, requiring [extremophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremophile "Extremophile") microorganisms with a range of tolerances, including thermophile (high temperature), psychrophile (low temperature), acidophile (high acidity), halophile (high salinity), oligotroph (low nutrient concentration), xerophile (dry environments) and radioresistant (high radiation tolerance) microorganisms. [Genetic engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_engineering "Genetic engineering") may produce polyextremophile microorganisms with several tolerances. The target atmospheres will probably lack oxygen, so the colonizers should include [anaerobic microorganisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaerobic_microorganisms "Anaerobic microorganisms"). Colonizing anaerobic [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria") may later establish atmospheric oxygen that is needed for higher [evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution "Evolution"), as it happened on Earth. Aerobic organisms in the biological payload may be delivered to the astronomical objects later when the conditions are right, by comets that captured and preserved the capsules.

The development of [eukaryote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote") microorganisms was a major bottleneck to higher evolution on Earth. Including eukaryote microorganisms in the payload can bypass this barrier. Multicellular organisms are even more desirable, but being much heavier than bacteria, fewer can be sent. Hardy [tardigrades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrades "Tardigrades") (water-bears) may be suitable but they are similar to [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropods "Arthropods") and would lead to insects. The body-plan of [rotifers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotifers "Rotifers") could lead to higher animals, if the rotifers can be hardened to survive interstellar transit.

Microorganisms or capsules captured in the accretion disc can be captured along with the dust into asteroids. During aqueous alteration the asteroids contain water, inorganic salts and organics, and [astroecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astroecology "Astroecology") experiments with meteorites showed that algae, bacteria, fungi and plant cultures can grow in the asteroids in these media.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Bioresources2-22) Microorganisms can then spread in the accreting solar nebula, and will be delivered to planets in comets and in asteroids. The microorganisms can grow on nutrients in the carrier comets and asteroids in the aqueous planetary environments, until they adapt to the local environments and nutrients on the planets.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-bioresources-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Bioresources2-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-23)

### Signal in the genome

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Signal in the genome")\]

A number of publications since 1979 have proposed the idea that directed panspermia could be demonstrated to be the origin of all life on Earth if a distinctive 'signature' message were found, deliberately implanted into either the [genome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome") or the [genetic code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_code "Genetic code") of the first microorganisms by our hypothetical progenitor.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-The_New_York_Times-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-27) In 2013 a team of physicists claimed that they had found mathematical and [semiotic patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiotics "Semiotics") in the genetic code which, they believe, is evidence for such a signature.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-29) This claim has not been substantiated by further study, or accepted by the wider scientific community. One outspoken critic is biologist [PZ Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PZ_Myers "PZ Myers") who said, writing in [Pharyngula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharyngula_/(blog/) "Pharyngula (blog)"):

> Unfortunately, what they’ve so honestly described is good old honest garbage ... Their methods failed to recognize a well-known functional association in the genetic code; they did not rule out the operation of natural law before rushing to falsely infer design ... We certainly don’t need to invoke panspermia. Nothing in the genetic code requires design, and the authors haven’t demonstrated otherwise.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-30)

In a later peer-reviewed article, the authors address the operation of natural law in an extensive statistical test, and draw the same conclusion as in the previous article.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-31) In special sections they also discuss methodological concerns raised by PZ Myers and some others.

Significantly, panspermia missions can be launched by present or near-future technologies. However, more advanced technologies may be also used when these become available. The biological aspects of directed panspermia may be improved by [genetic engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_engineering "Genetic engineering") to produce hardy polyextremophile microorganisms and multicellular organisms, suitable to diverse astronomical objects environments. Hardy polyextremophile anaerobic multicellular eukaryotes with high radiation resistance, that can form a self-sustaining ecosystem with [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), would combine ideally the features needed for survival and higher evolution.

For advanced missions, [ion thrusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_thrusters "Ion thrusters") or solar sails using [beam-powered propulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beam-powered_propulsion "Beam-powered propulsion") accelerated by Earth-based lasers can achieve speeds up to 0.01 _c_ (3×106 m/s). [Robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robots "Robots") may provide in-course navigation, may control the reviving of the frozen microbes periodically during transit to [repair radiation damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_repair "DNA repair"), and may also choose suitable targets. These propulsion methods and robotics are under development.

Microbial payloads may be also planted on hyperbolic [comets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comets "Comets") bound for interstellar space. This strategy follows the mechanisms of natural panspermia by comets, as suggested by Hoyle and Wikramasinghe.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-32) The microorganisms would be frozen in the comets at interstellar temperatures of a few [kelvins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") and protected from radiation for eons. It is unlikely that an ejected comet will be captured in another planetary system, but the probability can be increased by allowing the microbes to multiply during warm [perihelion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perihelion "Perihelion") approach to the Sun, then fragmenting the comet. A 1 km radius comet would yield 4.2×1012 one-kg seeded fragments, and rotating the comet would eject these shielded icy objects in random directions into the galaxy. This increases a trillion-fold the probability of capture in another planetary system, compared with transport by a single comet.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-SeedingBook-10)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner2-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12) Such manipulation of comets is a speculative long-term prospect.

The German physicist [Claudius Gros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius_Gros "Claudius Gros") has proposed that the technology developed by the [Breakthrough Starshot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Starshot "Breakthrough Starshot") initiative may be utilized in a second step to establish a [biosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosphere "Biosphere") of [unicellular microbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicellular_organism "Unicellular organism") on otherwise only transiently [habitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_habitability "Planetary habitability") [astronomical objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_object "Astronomical object").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Gros2016-33) The aim of this initiative, the Genesis project, would be to fast forward evolution to a stage equivalent of the [precambrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precambrian "Precambrian") period on Earth.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-34) Gros argues that the Genesis project would be realizable within 50–100 years,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Boddy2016-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-36) using low-mass probes equipped with a miniaturized gene laboratory for the _in situ_ [cell synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_cell "Artificial cell") of the microbes.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Callaway2016-37) The Genesis project extends directed panspermia to [eukaryotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote") life, arguing that it is more likely that complex life is rare,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-38) and not bacterial life. In 2020, the theoretical physicist [Avi Loeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avi_Loeb "Avi Loeb") wrote about a similar 3-D printer that can manufacture seeds of life in the _[Scientific American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_American "Scientific American")._[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-39)

Directed panspermia aims to secure and expand the family of organic gene/protein life. It may be motivated by the desire to perpetuate the common genetic heritage of all terrestrial life. This motivation was formulated as biotic ethics, that value the common gene/protein patterns of organic life,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner4-13) and as panbiotic ethics that aim to secure and expand life in the universe.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner2-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12)

[Molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology") shows complex patterns common to all cellular life, a common [genetic code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_code "Genetic code") and a common mechanism to [translate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_/(biology/) "Translation (biology)") it into [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein"), which in turn help to reproduce the DNA code. Also, shared are the basic mechanisms of energy use and material transport. These self-propagating patterns and processes are the core of organic gene/protein life. Life is unique because of this complexity, and because of the exact coincidence of the laws of physics that allow life to exist. Also unique to life is the pursuit of self-propagation, which implies a human purpose to secure and expand life. These objectives are best secured in space, suggesting a panbiotic ethics aimed to secure this future.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-SeedingBook-10)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner2-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner3-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-Mautner4-13)

Objections and counterarguments
-------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Directed_panspermia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Objections and counterarguments")\]

Directed panspermia may interfere with local life at the targets.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-40) The colonizing microorganisms may out-compete local life for resources, or infect and harm local organisms. However, this probability can be minimized by targeting newly forming planetary systems, accretion discs and star-forming clouds, where local life, and especially advanced life, could not have emerged yet. If there is local life that is fundamentally different, the colonizing microorganisms may not harm it. If there is local organic gene/protein life, it may exchange genes with the colonizing microorganisms, increasing galactic [biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity").

Another objection is that space should be left pristine for scientific studies, a reason for planetary quarantine. However, directed panspermia may reach only a few, at most a few hundred new stars, still leaving a hundred billion pristine for local life and for research. A technical objection is the uncertain survival of the messenger organisms during long interstellar transit. Research by simulations, and the development on hardy colonizers is needed to address these questions.

A third argument against engaging in directed panspermia derives from the view that wild animals do not — on the average — have lives worth living, and thus [spreading life would be morally wrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antinatalism "Antinatalism"). [Yew-Kwang Ng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yew-Kwang_Ng "Yew-Kwang Ng") supports this view.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-41) Unlike the above two objections, which can be minimized by attention to detail, there is no currently-known way to influence from a distance how evolution would progress on a world seeded with life. O'Brien argues that the large amount of suffering among wild animals on this planet is probably a result of the way evolution by natural selection operates, and that evolutionary processes are therefore likely to result, in due time, in similar suffering wherever life evolves.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-42) Sivula discusses all sides of the issue and concludes that "... the risk of suffering objection constitutes a serious ethical problem – planetary seeding may be extremely good or it might be a moral disaster – depending on one's moral theory. Until we have identified a satisfying resolution of this predicament, humanity should abstain from any acts of cosmic preservation."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-:0-3) Additionally, there is no guarantee that the future biospheres created will not suffer more than life has done on Earth.

The discovery of an ancient directed panspermia effort is the central theme of "[The Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chase_/(Star_Trek:_The_Next_Generation/) "The Chase (Star Trek: The Next Generation)")," a 1993 episode of _[Star Trek: The Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Next_Generation "Star Trek: The Next Generation")_. In the story, [Captain Picard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Picard "Captain Picard") must work to complete the penultimate research of his late archaeology professor's career. That professor, Galen, had discovered that [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") fragments seeded into the primordial genetic material of 19 worlds could be rearranged to assemble a [computer algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_algorithm "Computer algorithm"). Amid competition (and, later, with begrudging cooperation) from [Cardassian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardassian "Cardassian"), [Klingon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klingon "Klingon") and [Romulan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulan "Romulan") expeditions also exploring Galen's research clues, the _[Enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.S._Enterprise-D "U.S.S. Enterprise-D")_ crew discovers that an alien progenitor race had indeed, [4 billion years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiogenesis "Abiogenesis") prior, seeded genetic material across many star systems, thus directing the evolution of many humanoid species.

Some variation of directed panspermia was also included in the plot of [anime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime "Anime") _[Neon Genesis Evangelion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neon_Genesis_Evangelion "Neon Genesis Evangelion")_[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-43) and Ridley Scott's 2012 science fiction film _[Prometheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prometheus_/(2012_film/) "Prometheus (2012 film)")_.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_panspermia#cite_note-44)

[](https://github.com/taubyte/tau/edit/main/docs/platform/spore-drive.md "Edit this page")[](https://github.com/taubyte/tau/raw/main/docs/platform/spore-drive.md "View source of this page")

Spore Drive - Automated Deployment[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#spore-drive-automated-deployment "Permanent link")
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

While [manually deploying a Tau cloud](https://tau.how/platform/deployment/) gives you complete control over the setup process, automating this deployment can save significant time and reduce potential configuration errors. This is where Spore Drive comes in - a developer-friendly tool that automates cloud deployment with just a few lines of code.

### Why Spore Drive?[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#why-spore-drive "Permanent link")

While existing Infrastructure as Code (IaC) solutions could be used to deploy Tau, they often come with:

*   Complex configuration languages to learn
*   Steep learning curves
*   Heavy dependencies and prerequisites
*   Unnecessary features that add complexity

Spore Drive was created to align with Taubyte's philosophy of simplification. It provides:

*   A minimal, intuitive API that feels natural to developers
*   Just the features needed for Tau deployment
*   Agentless deployment using only SSH
*   Simple configuration through code

By focusing on simplicity and automation, Spore Drive lets you spend less time wrestling with infrastructure and more time building.

### Language Support[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#language-support "Permanent link")

While this guide uses TypeScript, Spore Drive is designed to be language-agnostic with:

*   Native Go support (core implementation)
*   TypeScript/JavaScript client
*   More clients coming soon (Python, Rust, etc.)

### How it works[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#how-it-works "Permanent link")

Spore drive is an RPC service that runs on your local machine. Unless used from browser, your SDK will start it for you.

[![Image 1](https://tau.how/images/spore-drive-overview-dia.png)](https://tau.how/images/spore-drive-overview-dia.png)

When your create a new configuration, spore-drive will create an instance of it either fully in memory if you don't provide a path or an in memory COW (Copy On Write) backed by a the file system. That allows multiple clients to manipulate the same configuration without having to worry about consistency. Only when you commit configuration changes, spore-drive will write the changes to the file system.

When you create a new drive, it takes a refrence to the configuration instance. When plot a course, a necessary step before deployment, spore-drive will create a plan of action to deploy tau.

Finally, when you call `displace`, spore drive, since it's agent-less, will use SSH to connect to your hosts and execute the deployment.

### Getting Started with TypeScript[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#getting-started-with-typescript "Permanent link")

Let's create a new project:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-0-1)$npminit-y
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-0-2)$npminstalltypescripttsx--save-dev
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-0-3)$npxtsc--init
```

Configure TypeScript in `tsconfig.json`:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-1){
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-2)"compilerOptions":{
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-3)"target":"ES2020",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-4)"module":"ESNext",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-5)"moduleResolution":"node",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-6)"declaration":true,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-7)"outDir":"dist",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-8)"rootDir":".",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-9)"strict":true,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-10)"esModuleInterop":true,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-11)"resolveJsonModule":true,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-12)"skipLibCheck":true,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-13)"lib":["ES2020"]
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-14)},
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-15)"include":["src/**/*.ts"],
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-16)"exclude":["node_modules"]
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-1-17)}
```

Add the run script to `package.json`:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-2-1)"scripts":{
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-2-2)"displace":"tsx src/index.ts"
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-2-3)},
```

Install Spore Drive:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-3-1)$npminstall@taubyte/spore-drive
```

### Writing the Deployment Code[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#writing-the-deployment-code "Permanent link")

Create `src/index.ts`:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-1)import{
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-2)Config,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-3)CourseConfig,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-4)Drive,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-5)TauLatest,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-6)Course,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-4-7)}from"@taubyte/spore-drive";
```

Initialize configuration:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-5-1)constconfig:Config=newConfig(`${__dirname}/../config`);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-5-2)awaitconfig.init();
```

> **Note**: If you ommit the path to configuration, it'll be stored in memory. Storing the `config` locally, especially in a git repository, is best practice.

Configure your cloud (similar to the manual setup in the previous guide):

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-1)exportconstcreateConfig=async(config:Config)=>{
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-2)// Set root domain (like enterprise.starships.ws from the manual guide)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-3)constdomain=config.Cloud().Domain();
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-4)awaitdomain.Root().Set("enterprise.starships.ws");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-5)awaitdomain.Generated().Set("e.ftll.ink");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-6)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-7)// Generate required keys (domain validation and swarm)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-8)awaitdomain.Validation().Generate();
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-6-9)awaitconfig.Cloud().P2P().Swarm().Generate();
```

Followed by configuring SSH access:

Using password authUsing key auth

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-7-1)// Configure SSH access
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-7-2)constmainAuth=config.Auth().Signer("main");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-7-3)awaitmainAuth.Username().Set("root");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-7-4)awaitmainAuth.Password().Set(process.env.HOST_PASSWORD!);
```

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-8-1)// Configure SSH access
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-8-2)constmainAuth=config.Auth().Signer("main");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-8-3)awaitmainAuth.Username().Set("root");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-8-4)awaitmainAuth.Key().Data().Set(awaitfs.promises.readFile(process.env.HOST_KEY!));
```

Then define your shapes. Here we're defining a `compute` shape.

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-1)// Define services (similar to manual configuration)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-2)constall=config.Shapes().Shape("compute");
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-3)awaitall.Services().Set([
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-4)"auth","tns","hoarder","seer",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-5)"substrate","patrick","monkey"
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-6)]);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-7)awaitall.Ports().Port("main").Set(BigInt(4242));
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-8)awaitall.Ports().Port("lite").Set(BigInt(4247));
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-9-9)}
```

Define your hosts list:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-1)// Define your hosts list with required fields
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-2)constyourHostsList=[
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-3){
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-4)ip:"1.2.3.4",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-5)id:"node-1",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-6)location:{
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-7)lat:40.076897,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-8)long:-109.33771,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-9)},
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-10)},
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-11){
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-12)ip:"5.6.7.8",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-13)id:"node-2",
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-14)location:{
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-15)lat:34.052235,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-16)long:-118.243683,
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-17)},
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-18)},
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-10-19)];
```

> **Note**: If you'd like an example of fetching hosts from a cloud provider, check out the [digitalocean-displacement](https://github.com/taubyte/digitalocean-displacement/tree/main) repository.

Add hosts (automatically configures what you'd manually set up):

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-1)constbootstrapers=[];
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-2)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-3)for(consthostofyourHostsList){
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-4)consthostname=`host-${host.id}-enterprise-starships`;
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-5)if(!hosts.includes(hostname)){
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-6)consthostConfig=config.Hosts().Host(hostname);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-7)bootstrapers.push(hostname);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-8)awaithostConfig.Addresses().Add([`${host.ip}/32`]);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-9)awaithostConfig.SSH().Address().Set(`${host.ip}:22`);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-10)awaithostConfig.SSH().Auth().Add(["main"]);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-11)awaithostConfig.Location().Set(host.location);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-12)if(!(awaithostConfig.Shapes().List()).includes("compute"))
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-13)awaithostConfig.Shapes().Shape("compute").Instance().Generate();
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-14)}
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-15)}
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-16)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-17)awaitconfig
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-18).Cloud()
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-19).P2P()
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-20).Bootstrap()
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-21).Shape("compute")
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-22).Nodes()
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-23).Add(bootstrapers);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-11-24)awaitconfig.Commit();
```

### Deploying Your Cloud[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#deploying-your-cloud "Permanent link")

Create and initialize the Drive:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-12-1)constdrive:Drive=newDrive(config,TauLatest);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-12-2)awaitdrive.init();
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-12-3)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-12-4)// Plot the deployment course
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-12-5)constcourse=awaitdrive.plot(newCourseConfig(["compute"]));
```

Start deployment:

```
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-1)// Start deployment
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-2)awaitcourse.displace();
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-3)
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-4)// Monitor progress
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-5)forawait(constprogressofawaitcourse.progress()){
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-6)console.log(`${progress.path}: ${progress.progress}%`);
[](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#__codelineno-13-7)}
```

### Full Example[¶](https://tau.how/platform/spore-drive/#full-example "Permanent link")

For a complete working example, check out our [step-by-step tutorial](https://dev.to/samyfodil/build-your-cloud-2nmm) that walks through deploying a Tau cloud on DigitalOcean using Spore Drive.

News and Media

*   Pamela Silver elected to National Academy of Sciences
    -----------------------------------------------------
    
    May 8, 2023
    
    Systems and synthetic biology pioneer and Wyss Core Faculty member Pamela Silver appointed to distinguished Academy of government advisors. [Read the full article.](https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/pamela-silver-elected-to-national-academy-of-sciences/)
    
*   Four researchers with MIT ties earn 2023 Schmidt Science Fellowships
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    
    Four researchers with ties to MIT have been named Schmidt Science Fellows this year. Lillian Chin ’17, SM ’19; Neil Dalvie PD ’22, PhD ’22; Suong Nguyen, and Yirui Zhang SM ’19, PhD ’23 are among the 32 exceptional early-career scientists worldwide chosen to receive the prestigious fellowships. [Read the Article Here](https://news.mit.edu/2023/four-researchers-mit-ties-earn-schmidt-science-fellowships-0512)
    

*   Sam Lim on Protecting Plants with Proteins
    ------------------------------------------
    
    Like the organisms he studies, Sam Lim has been able to thrive in a variety of environments. He was born in Indiana, moved to Seoul, Korea at age two, spent his undergraduate years in Massachusetts, and did his Ph.D. in the San Francisco Bay Area. Now, he’s hoping to use the proteins that enable tardigrades, or water bears, to survive in harsh ecosystems to protect plants from extreme conditions, like drought. Learn more about Sam and his work in this month’s [Humans of the Wyss.](https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/humans-of-the-wyss-sam-lim-on-protecting-plants-with-proteins/)
    
*   Bacterial Biosensors Eavesdrop on the Gut
    -----------------------------------------
    
    Genetically engineered bacteria could help diagnose or monitor gut diseases. [Read more here.](https://www.drugdiscoverynews.com/bacterial-biosensors-eavesdrop-on-the-gut-15641)
    
*   IUBMB Jubilee Award Lectures
    ----------------------------

    Read the article [HERE](https://iubmb.org/activities/iubmb-awards-and-lectures/jubilee-lecturers/?_hsenc=p2ANqtz-_w504cFxs82XExv-BAyRivj9F37RDJuZyQiS4ByNd_ERPZBGanLpPJoj6AbcsLx9HNThebuGQjcFnGg6CQ3V_NGXL-mQ8aGlrrYTthUj16PWIIJiY&_hsmi=247988652&utm_content=247988652&utm_medium=email&utm_source=hs_email)

She has managed to successfully translate many of her scientific achievements into entrepreneurship, product commercialization, and collaborations with companies whose goals align with hers. It specifically focuses on our recent 2022 paper from Veling, et al.: [Natural and Designed Proteins Inspired by Extremotolerant Organisms Can Form Condensates and Attenuate Apoptosis in Human Cells](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acssynbio.1c00572)

    -------------------------------------------------------------------

    [**Read the report**](https://asm.org/ASM/media/Academy/Academy%20Reports/Microbes-Climate-Change-Science,-People-Impacts-Report.pdf)

*   Engineered microbes make silver nanoparticles
    ---------------------------------------------
    
    in [c&en](https://cen.acs.org/index.html), 5 July 2016
    
    To make these minuscule metal globs, [Pamela A. Silve](https://silver.med.harvard.edu/index.php/pasilver/)r and Tobias W. Giessen of Harvard University turned to a 20-sided capsulelike structure in bacteria known as encapsulin, which holds iron-storing proteins that pack the capsule full of iron. The researchers removed the gene that encodes encapsulin’s iron-storing protein from Thermotoga maritima bacteria and replaced it with the sequence for a short protein that precipitates elemental silver instead. Then they transferred the entire genetic piece into an easy-to-grow laboratory strain of Escherichia coli. As a result, these structures in the engineered E. coli stuffed themselves with silver from their growth medium, forming symmetrical nanoparticles about 13 to 15 nm in diameter. The team broke open the cells to isolate and purify the nanoparticles.

==================================================================================

The ability to instantaneously jump from one location in space to another clearly violates the laws of physics. Or does it?

[![Image 4: Ethan Siegel](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*JE2i36RVA_8ejCr2F5ZtNA.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@startswithabang?source=post_page---byline--8c49e5d5af36---------------------------------------)
